subtopic: FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE STANDS

speechtext:
Mr. HUGHES CLEAVER (Halton) presented the first report of the special committee on war expenditures, as follows: Your committee recommends that it be empowered:
1.	To sit while the house is sitting and notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place.

War Expenditures Committee
2.	To determine the manner and extent to which the evidence, proceedings and reports shall be printed or typed, and that where the same are ordered to be printed there be printed 500 copies in English and 200 copies in French, and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.
3.	To appoint subcommittees, to fix the quorum of any such subcommittee, and to refer to such subcommittee any of the matters referred to the committee; any subcommittee so appointed to have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses under oath or otherwise, to sit while the house is sitting and notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, to adjourn from place to place, and to report from time to time to the committee.
4.	To employ such secretarial, reportorial, clerical and other assistance as it may deem necessary.
5.	In cases where considerations of national security preclude the publishing of certain recommendations and of the arguments upon which they are based, to address a memorandum to the Prime Minister for the consideration of the war cabinet, provided that the committee shall, whenever it has exercised such powers, report the fact as soon as possible to the house.
Your committee further recommends that during any adjournment of the house, its reports shall be deemed to have been tabled when filed with the clerk of the house and seven days have elapsed after the date of such filing.
Your committee further recommends that six members constitute a quorum, and that standing order 65 (3) be suspended in relation thereto.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Mr. CLEAVER moved that the report be concurred in.

subtopic: SALE OF WHEAT TO CANADIAN MILLS
speechtext:
The Canadian mills buy the great bulk of their wheat requirements on the Winnipeg grain exchange. The Canadian wheat board is one of the sellers on that market and makes its sales at the ruling market prices. Likewise, the mills buying in the futures market could not separate purchases from the board and purchases from other sellers.

The public has a perfect right to know what is being censored so far as this country is concerned. Even in war time there cannot be

The public has a right to know what the government is doing with respect to censorship. There is confusion and conflict on every hand with regard to this matter. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DELAY IN DELIVERIES TO WESTERN CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DELAY IN DELIVERIES TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I was anxious to direct a question to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), but when I got in touch with his department I found that he would be unavoidably absent to-day. Therefore I desire to direct the question to the Minister of Finance, and I wish he would see the proper authorities and perhaps make a statement to-morrow. It is with respect to a serious situation which has developed in western Canada in regard to binder twine. I have received letters from two different firms, one an implement company and the other a hardware company, and to put the case clearly I should like to quote briefly from one letter, coming from a merchant at Langbank, Saskatchewan:
I have to-day received a letter from the Brantford Cordage Company, Winnipeg, regarding a car of binder twine which was ordered in June for immediate shipment. The company states that the dominion government have un expectedly and without previous notice taken over from the Canadian manufacturers four million pounds of binder twine . . . and that it was necessary for this company to turn over all stocks of twine already at the head of the lakes.
He goes on to say that fall rye will be ready to harvest early in August, and that the situation will be serious if they cannot get binder twine. Will the minister look into the situation and make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DELAY IN DELIVERIES TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I understand the acting minister has a reply ready.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Acting Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DELAY IN DELIVERIES TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member sent notice to the department, and a reply was prepared and placed in my hands, as acting minister.
At the beginning of July an urgent request was received from the British raw materials board for the supply of 4,400,000 pounds of binder twine to meet a shortage which had arisen in the United Kingdom owing to an exceptionally early and heavy crop. The Department of Agriculture agreed to the release of this binder twine, and immediate steps were taken by the general purchasing branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply to requisition the necessary amount. It was found that insufficient quantities were on hand in the plants in eastern Canada, and large amounts had to be shipped from the head of the lakes. This caused a temporary

dislocation of distribution in the western provinces, but will not result in any delay in deliveries to the farmers when the binder twine is needed. The British authorities have agreed to release immediately to Canada sufficient fibre to replace the twine shipped to England, and Canadian manufacturers are making every effort to increase their production of binder twine to avoid any possible shortage in Canada for the 1943 crop.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 132, to facilitate compromises and arrangements between insolvent farmers and their creditors.
He said: In February 1943, the judicial committee of the privy council held that the Alberta Debt Adjustment Act, 1937, was legislation in relation to insolvency and constituted a substantial invasion of the exclusive legislative powers of the parliament of Canada in relation to bankruptcy and insolvency and obstructed and interfered with the actual legislation of that parliament on those matters, and therefore was ultra vires. The decisions of the privy council served to confirm the decisions of the lower courts on the Saskatchewan Debt Adjustment Act and
likewise threw grave doubts upon the Manitoba Debt Adjustment Act.
As a result, representations were made to the dominion government by various delegations, including a delegation from the Saskatoon conference of representatives of the three prairie province governments and farmers' organizations and representatives of the mortgage and investment companies and insurance companies, as well as other individual creditors and debtors. Various representations were made to the government from private citizens of the prairie provinces, including a considerable number of farmers who represented the point of view of both debtors and vendors of land. The need for a means of adjusting the old and onerous debt loads of depressed farmers in the west was admitted, but various opinions were advanced as to the best method of doing this. I think it is fair to say that general emphasis was iput on the importance of safeguarding the credit of western agriculture and ensuring the necessary flow of new capital for the development of that industry. The position of the farmer as a potential creditor was emphasized, for instance, the case where an older farmer wishes to retire and sell his farm under an agreement for sale to a young man about to start in farming.
Experience has shown certain limitations of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, and it was urged upon the government by representatives of both debtors and creditors that these defects should be remedied by new legislation under the bankruptcy jurisdiction of the dominion. Manitoba pressed for the extension of the act, or similar legislation, to that province as well as to Alberta and Saskatchewan, and indeed the Saskatoon conference suggested that there be enacted legislation which would provide for continuous adjustment of farm debts.
The government has given careful consideration to these representations and to the question of the best way of meeting the problem that existed in the three prairie provinces without doing irreparable harm to the credit of western agriculture. After careful deliberation, the government reached the decision that it was inadvisable at this time to reopen the fundamental issues of the western debt problem. To embark upon legislation so highly controversial during the stress of war, when the energies of parliament and the country as a whole are being taxed by immediate war emergencies, was felt to be unwise. A constructive solution of the particular problem of western debt, and of the problem of agricultural credit generally, should be attempted only when we can see more clearly the conditions that are likely
Farmers' Creditors Act

to prevail after the war. Moreover there is already on the statute books the Central Mortgage Bank Act, passed in 1939, and designed to provide a permanent solution of the farm debt problem, while at the same time safeguarding the credit of the farmers and ensuring that the future capital needs of the farming industry would be met and at moderate interest rates. Owing to the outbreak of war in September 1939, this act has never been brought into force, and it was considered inadvisable to implement it during the war years because of the uncertainties which the war interjected into such fundamental matters as the values of farm lands and the real value of farm income. Moreover, it was considered that the national credit must be utilized to the full in the prosecution of the war.
The government, however, felt it desirable to meet the immediate need of preventing farmers from being dispossessed of their lands when food production was of such vital importance to the nation, and to that end an order in council was passed following the announcement of the privy council decisions, which provided that in any action by a mortgagee for foreclosure, or by a vendor under an agreement for sale or cancellation of the agreement, the court may stay the action, postpone the payment of any moneys due, vary or extend any order previously made with a view to retaining on the land during the state of war now existing an efficient and industrious farmer and at the same time protecting all other persons having any interest in the land of the debtor.
At the same time the study which has been made of the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, and of the representations received earlier this year, has induced us to introduce the bill which is now before the house. This bill is designed to rescind the 1934 act and substitute for it an act which will continue, with important changes, the system of farm debt adjustment which has on the whole worked successfully in the past. I shall call attention to the more important changes. The bill extends the system of farmer-debt adjustment to Manitoba, retains the limiting date line of May 1, 1935, but provides that if two-thirds of a farmer's debts were incurred prior to that date he may seek an adjustment of all his debts including those incurred subsequent to that date; allows cases to be reopened where farmers made a composition prior to January 1, 1939, and establishes a new machinery for the administration of the act by substituting for the boards of review the county or district courts of Jhe provinces with appeals to a single judge of the superior or appeal courts of the province.

That is a brief statement of the principles of the bill. I presume there will be some discussion of those principles, and at the conclusion of the debate, if it is not too long, I may have something further to say.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the example of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) I do not intend on this occasion to speak at length. Taking the measure as a whole, I believe it represents an endeavour on the part of the government to meet a condition the seriousness of which has not been much lessened in western Canada with the passage of years. With the point of view he expressed, that there is a desire to assist a farmer who may find himself in a difficult position owing to circumstances over which in the main he has had no control, I agree. I agree also with the principle that the credit of the farmer, in his own interests, should be considered.
This is a most important piece of legislation, in that it is intended to bring up to date legislation introduced by Mr. Bennett in the house on June 4, 1934. At that time he pointed out the purposes for which it was intended. This is what he said:
We should endeavour to secure a cheap and speedy method by which a farmer in difficulty could provide some arrangement or composition with his creditors. It is a well-known fact to members of the house engaged in business that under the common law no compromise could be made with a man by his creditors to pay less than one hundred cents on the dollar unless all creditors agree.
Later in his speech he said:
The object, of course, is to keep the farmer on the farm; if possible to keep him cultivating the land upon which he has lived. In making the arrangement we contemplate, through the assistance of those who have loaned him money, it follows of course that we can go only a certain distance in determining how his security can be dealt with.
When the bill came before the house certain changes were made in it, and during the years in which it has been in effect since 1934 it has afforded much assistance to the western farmer. In many cases it has spelled the difference between continuing or discontinuing farming operations. We had difficulties in Saskatchewan during the years 1931-1936 by reason of crop failures, low prices, which placed the farmers in such a position that they could not pay their debts. Conditions were not as acute subsequently as they had been prior to 1934 when the act was passed; nevertheless, however honest a farmer may have been, and however desirous he was of paying he could not during these years meet his liabilities. And I want to say here and now to some who assert that the western

Farmers' Creditors Act
farmer has not been honest in his debt relationships, that there is no foundation for the suggestion; for during the past year or two, when the farmer has found himself in a better financial condition than he had been in for a period of years, he has been meeting his debts in a manner and to a degree that has not been excelled in any other part of this country.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He will always pay when he can.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
As the leader of
the opposition says, the farmer will always pay his debts when he can. But during a period of eight or ten years such as he passed through, with no crops or small crops in some years, and with low prices in the years when he had good crops, it was impossible for the farmer to pay.
Now we come to the war period. While there has been an increase in the income of the farmer since the war began, that increase does not assure him of an income equal to what he had in the years 1926 to 1929. This legislation is important because it is one method whereby the war effort of this dominion may be assisted. It is actually in the nature of a war measure, although it will be effective after the war. Production must be kept at a height commensurate with the great demands of our army overseas, of our people in Canada, and of the other nations. The overwhelming load of debt that even now rests on the western farmer is in its nature detrimental to maximum production.
I shall not go into much detail, except to say that up to April of 1940 there were 5,094 proposals made under the act since 1935; secured debts were reduced by 118,547,051 and unsecured debts by $1,926,819 during that period, or an average reduction of 41-9 per cent per farm. In the province of Saskatchewan there were 142,000 farmers with a debt load in excess of $482,000,000 according to a computation made some time ago by Doctor Hope of the university of Saskatchewan. That is a tremendous load of debt, and the result of it has been to destroy hope in the hearts of many who would have desired to continue as farmers. They have had the opportunity of coming before the boards of review in Saskatchewan and in the western provinces, other than Manitoba. Manitoba has not been under the act for some considerable time, and debts have been written down. But the act up to the present time has not covered certain situations that it should cover. So intense has the movement become in the western provinces for a reconsideration of the debt problem that the submission to the federal government in
1943, to which the minister referred, asked for the setting up of a tribunal or tribunals, to be created by proper legislative authority, in order to:
(a)	Write down the principal of farm debts, secured and unsecured.
(b)	Reduce the interest rate on farm debts, secured and unsecured.
(c)	Alter the terms of payment of farm debts, secured and unsecured.
(d)	Review and revise its own decisions in the light of events subsequent to the making of the decision.
(e)	Extend to individuals in any particular year or circumstances, the protection of any of the provisions of this legislation available to any debtor whose affairs are being administered under it.
(f)	Stay proceedings arising on debts or securities after an adjudication has been made.
(g)	Make the foregoing remedies available with respect to any farm debts regardless of the time at which they were incuri'ed.
That submission was made in March, 1943.
The minister has mentioned that the debt adjustment act of Alberta was declared beyond the powers of the legislature. It was felt that the debt adjustment acts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba would be in the same position; therefore the government was requested to consider legislation in the form of an order in council to be passed under the War Measures Act in order to protect farmer debtors against foreclosure and cancellation. An order in council was passed by the governor in council along the lines of section 15 of a Saskatchewan statute known as the Limitation of Civil Rights Act. I shall not discuss the details of that order in council, but under it provision was made that in actions by a mortgagee for foreclosure or by a vendor of land for cancellation of an agreement of sale the judge might, after making inquiries con-, cerning the income and assets of the parties and all other relevant matters, grant a stay of execution, postpone payment of any moneys due, and prescribe terms and conditions to which any order shall be subject.
I believe that the legislation before us, except for some changes that I should like to suggest, will go a long way towards meeting the farmer-debtor's position in the western provinces, provided that the order in council is kept in effect to operate alongside of the new act. I repeat the order in council must be retained. I would rather it were incorporated as part of the present statute, but if the government refuses to do that and wishes to continue it in effect under the War Measures Act, I shall have no serious objection to that course. It will be in effect only for the period of the war, and it may be justifiable under the circumstances to have it in the form of an order in council. But I would

Farmers' Creditors Act
point out that if the order in council is allowed to lapse-and in the province of Saskatchewan there is no effective debt adjustment act; the Alberta Act was declared ultra vires-serious results wil' follow in the matter of the loss of land by foreclosure and cancellation, in eases where the farmer is entitled to be kept on the land as being an efficient producer, although his inability to pay is due to conditions under which he has no control.
I think commendation is due for making provision for an appeal from the decision of the district court judges, who now will take the position of administering the act. One principle which must be upheld is the right of an individual to appeal, for the purpose of having his rights established and his rights secured from administrative bodies, whether headed by a judge or any other person; otherwise orders arbitrary in their effect may be made. To make no allowance for appeal would be a denial of justice. Provision has been made for that, and I think it is a worthy provision. I also think that the inclusion of estates, by allowing executors or administrators to seek adjustment of debts, is also worthy of commendation. I feel however 'that provision should be made whereby executors or administrators, the personal representatives of deceased estates, should be permitted to apply for a readjustment irrespective of the date of the death of the decedent in the estate.
He has just mentioned the fact that the date line for the application of the act to personal representatives goes back to July 3, 1934. I ask him to give consideration to extending that date line still further beyond that date. He has mentioned that provision has been made for allowing the reopening of cases which came before the board of review prior to January 1, 1939. That, too, is a worthwhile step. The great difficulty in connection with the administration of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been that there has been no general principle, or body of jurisprudence -if I may be allowed to apply that to the orders of a board of review-brought into being. One of the great objections to the board has been that in certain cases there have been tremendous writeoffs and reductions and in other cases in the same locality, where farmers were entitled to similar writeoffs, the reductions have been less. The result has been a feeling of inequality and inequity which will now, I believe, be done away with by reason of the fact that a right of appeal has been set up which will ensure uniformity of administration all over the province. This provision for appeal is worthy of high commendation. I

repeat that if one thing is more important than another in an act such as this, and for that matter in all legislation, it is that there shall be equality of application and administration as much as is humanly possible.
I shall refer to various other matters when the sections are taken up; we shall come to that in the discussion in committee. With the general principle of the bill I agree. With the changes which have been made, the alterations in set-up, I feel that a forward step has been made. I think that if the act is properly applied, if an invitation is given to farmers who, through no fault of their own, find themselves unable to meet their debts, to take advantage of the act, it is-subject to certain objections which I shall take later on-a measure which goes a considerable way towards relieving the difficulties of farmers who are in debt in the western provinces. I know there are those who will say it should go much further. I too could say that, Mr. Speaker, for I feel that in certain directions it does not go far enough. But having regard to all the circumstances, to the need of legislation being passed, to the fact that the government has seen fit to go so far and will, I suppose, go no further, and that there is in this legislation some hope for the farmer who is in difficulty, who is honest and straightforward and desires to pay his debts if only he has the income so to do, I am going to support this bill. It is a step in the right direction.
The government should appoint the most outstanding judge in each of the provinces who can be made available for the purposes of administering this act by way of appeal. It will depend in its application and its administration, not so much on the letter of the law, but rather upon the judge who will be charged with being the appeal court, whose decision will be final. It places a large responsibility in the hands of one judge. If the judge who is chosen is an outstanding judge, appreciative of the terrible difficulties through which the western farmer has passed through a period of some twelve or fourteen years, realizing the necessity that something must be done and that a liberal interpretation should be given the provisions of this act, then I feel that much good will be done. On the other hand, if the administration of the act is placed in the hands of a judge who will not give a liberal interpretation, while the act may promise much, it will effect little actual good. I do ask that the minister give us during the debate, an opportunity to find out who the judge will be in each of the provinces. I do not think there is anything unfair in that suggestion. The judge will be

Farmers' Creditors Act
charged with being the custodian of the future of western agriculture, and in Saskatchewan there are 140,000 farmers. In setting up the administrative boards, in setting up an appeal court, parliament has the right to know who will be appointed, the right to discuss the appointee's qualifications, and the right to inform the minister and the country whether or not the appointees whom the government has in mind will meet with the approval of those who will be most affected, namely, the farmers.
I ask the minister to give the house and the country an assurance that the order in council passed under the War Measures Act will be continued in effect until the end of the war. For unless that order in council is continued in effect, while there will be legislation provided for the writing down of debts, and for the granting of extensions where the farmer comes under the act, there will be no protection for the farmer such as was guaranteed to him under the provisions of the debt adjustment act.

speechtext:
In considering the problem of farm debt it is well to remember at all times that this problem exists to a very large extent as a result of the failure of federal governments in the past to maintain a sound national policy, especially in its relationship to western agriculture. I think it is well also to remember that western Canada was not opened up especially for the benefit of the people who settled there, nor for the benefit of the west, but to a considerable extent for the benefit of the central provinces, and if you will read Hansard of 1903 and 1905, taking the speeches of Clifford Sifton and Frank Oliver, that becomes perfectly plain.
I would say that a national policy which forces any class of society, and I have the farmers in mind, to sell their products at world market prices, while on the other hand incurring their costs in a highly-protected market, brings about a condition that is almost certain to lead to the bankruptcy of that class of people. And that of course is exactly what happened in the years from 1930 to 1939. The failure of the federal government in those years to pass legislation to protect the farmers against those conditions brought the provincial governments into the field, and protective legislation was put into effect for the purposes, as far as possible, of guaranteeing the security of tenure of the farmers. That legislation, -while it was incapable of bringing about a compulsory reduction in the amount of debts owed, did nevertheless give the farmers a bargaining power, and as a result of that legislation, many farmers were able, by mutual agreement with
their creditors, to get a reduction of their debts, because the creditors did not have the power to force farmers off their land or to seize their chattels.
The decision of the privy council in wiping out the provincial debt legislation has, I am afraid, a little weakened the people's faith in the administration of law and justice in western Canada. In that regard I would quote from the Hanna Herald, which by no stretch of the imagination can be called a radical paper. It is a very orthodox one. In the edition of March 11 appeared this editorial:
Nevertheless it must be admitted that the disallowance of the Alberta debt legislation has not been received with approbation by the majority of Alberta people. Whatever the defects of the method undertaken, the people of this province always had the idea that they had the right to run their own aifairs in this respect at least. A large number of Alberta people are coming to the conclusion that the courts of justice are always on the side of property rights in that they will consider such rights ahead of the welfare of the people. It may be that is what the law says. We do not know. But we do know that it will be an unfortunate day for the whole judicial set-up in Canada if the people of the west come to the conclusion that the courts will always be against them when concentrated wealth is on the other side.
I would add, Mr. Speaker, that when the people's faith in the administration of law and justice in any country is destroyed, you are paving the way for internal strife.
Now it is up to the federal government to deal with the matter. The provinces apparently, for the time being at any rate, are out of the picture. And so we come to this bill. In my opinion, after reading the bill through very carefully, it does seem that the government has almost entirely disregarded the recommendations of the western debt conference and given way to the recommendations or pressure of the mortgage companies.
I will give three examples to show where, in my opinion, the federal government has definitely sided with the mortgage companies against the three western provinces: Substituting courts for boards of review, thereby increasing costs to the farmers, and also doing away with a great deal of the sympathetic consideration which they have received of recent years from the type of commissioners appointed to these boards. Failure to treat debt as a recurring problem, and that was strongly emphasized by the western debt conference, and it was also fought quite strenuously, on the other hand, by the mortgage companies. The government apparently has decided to side with the mortgage companies on that question. Then the right of appeal against the decision of the court. That will further add to the costs of the farmers. The inclusion of Manitoba is

they come home, they find that as a result of their enlistment their fathers were not able to carry on efficiently and the farms were sold over the heads of the older men? I am satisfied they will feel that they have done only half their job in fighting overseas, that there is another battle to be fought out in this country. Why should any boy be asked to go overseas and perhaps sacrifice his life for his country while we have a bunch of bloodsuckers of this kind doing everything in their power to have the government give them the right to seize the farms of men who, just because their sons have gone away, are not able to operate efficiently? Neither of these pamphlets contains one word in regard to the situation which has been brought about by the enlistment of these boys throughout the west, and the recommendations coming from the west in this regard have been ignored. I should say that the only justification for refusing to deal with a debtor should be either dishonesty or rank idleness; those should be the only two reasons.
The mortgage companies very bitterly oppose permanent debt adjustment machinery. In this connection I would quote from page 7 of another pamphlet issued by these companies, entitled "The Prairie Farmer and His Debts," as follows:
It is often urged that peculiar and specialized western conditions make the lot of western farmers more difficult and uncertain than that of the farmers in the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, and that, for this reason, permanent mortgage debt adjustment machinery, having power to revise and reduce debts indefinitely or periodically, must be provided. This argument will not stand up under examination. . . . The contention that western agriculture is more hazardous is based on the assumption that all western farms are almost entirely dependent upon wheat production and are what are generally called "grain" farms. The production figures and the 1936 census classification of farm holdings disprove this. The majority of farms in Manitoba and Alberta are certainly not grain farms.
Manitoba farmers secured only 21-7 per cent of their 1942 cash income from wheat; Saskatchewan farmers, 39-4 per cent; and Alberta farmers, 24-2 per cent. According to the 1936 census, 125.583 farms, or 42 per cent of the total, are under 200 acres in size. These farms, comparable in size to eastern farms, should be considered as diversified farm units and as economic units are similar to mixed farms in eastern Canada. Many of the larger farms are also engaged in mixed farming. There are 45.939 farms over 640 acres in size. These are essentially large-scale business enterprises.
Well, I think it would be hard to find anywhere a paragraph as short as that one containing as many completely misleading statements-in fact, I might say so many misstatements of fact. It states that the
majority of farmers to-day are not grain farmers. But in making that statement the reference is to the year 1942, when, as all hon. members know, there was a quota on wheat; therefore the farmer was not able to sell the total amount of his wheat in any one year, and naturally his income from wheat was reduced. If a comparison between wheat and live stock income in western Canada is to be made, then surely the comparison should be with income from these sources before the wheat quotas were put into force. If we do that, again referring to the pamphlet issued by the Manitoba federation of agriculture, we find at page 10 that in 1939 sixty-three per cent of the farmers' income was derived from wheat. That is very different from the 21 per cent stated by the mortgage companies.
That, however is not my chief point. I have dealt with it only to. refute their suggestion. My main point is that the mortgage companies try to stress the point that the majority of farms are diversified, and that therefore in respect of hazard they can be compared favourably w'ith farms in eastern Canada. I wonder what the people who drew up this pamphlet really think that stock in western Canada lives on. Do they think stock lives on hot air? When there is a drought the grain crop and the hay is destroyed. What do these individuals think the stock lives on? It cannot live on stones and water alone. It is only necessary to go back to the years 1936 and 1937, when the great drought hit western Canada, and when live stock became a distinct liability, to understand the situation. What happened? The situation became so serious that a lot of stock had to be moved out. Feed had to be moved into that area. Before the federal government would move feed into the drought area for the farmers, every farmer obtaining feed was forced to cut down his stock to three or four head per family.
What did he get for that stock in those days? What did he get for it between 1935 and 1937? Perhaps in that connection I might read from a statement which appeared in The Budget, issued by the Alberta Wheat Pool on May 29, 1943. This is what they say: Cattle Prices Then and Now
Good money is being obtained for cattle at the present time but during the 1930's cattle raising was most unprofitable and those who were engaged in it suffered heavy losses. As proof we reprint the following dispatch which appeared in newspapers some eight years ago:
"Edmonton, February 22, 1935-An average net return of only $1,174 a head was obtained by the provincial government on sales of 9,881
(Mr. Quelch.]

head of cattle purchased in the drought areas of the province last year, it was revealed in a return brought down in the legislature by Hon. F. S. Grisdale, minister of agriculture.
The return showed that 6,535 of these cattle were brought to Edmonton at a transportation cost of $13,050 and sold for $20,856, or an average of $1.19 a head. Total number of cattle shipped to Calgary was 3,346 at a transportation cost of $7,284. Sales of these cattle yielded $11,319 or $1.22 a head."
When the mortgage companies suggest therefore, that since western Canada is now becoming diversified there is no longer any hazard, it shows just how little they understand the western situation.
The last sentence of the paragraph I read a moment ago is just as misleading as the rest of it, when it says that there are 45,939 farms over 640 acres in size, and that these are essentially large-scale business enterprises. Anyone familiar with the dry belt of the west knows that practically all the farms in that area are of 640 acres or over, and that many of them are over 3,000 acres. And, they are not large business enterprises; they are just ordinary farms. If one is farming in that area he has to have a large one, if he is to make a living at all. And those men need consideration, just as much as the farmers on the half-sections in the park belt, or elsewhere.
Therefore I say it is quite evident that unless the government is prepared to stabilize prices at a fair level, bring down a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance and take steps to adjust debts at the present time, debt legislation to deal with debt as a recurring problem will have to be brought down. If that were done I would be willing to see all farm debt legislation done away with. I should be glad to see the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act repealed, and no more debt legislation brought down, in the event of those measures being taken, because I believe we would then have solved the problem. But until that problem is solved, the question of debt will have to be regarded as one which will recur from time to time.
Another point, and one which the minister referred to and which is emphasized by mortgage companies, is that mortgage debt legislation destroys credit. It is well to remember that debt legislation is an effect, not a cause. The cause is depression and drought. Stabilize farm prices, institute crop insurance, and to a very large extent you will be stabilizing credit, because you will be removing the hazards connected with lending money in western Canada. But until that is done it will continue to be a hazardous procedure. Do not place the blame upon debt legislation; place it where it fairly belongs, namely upon
the hazards to western Canada as represented by low prices, drought and the like.

The house resumed at three o'clock.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in closing I wish to make a few remarks regarding the funds of the mortgage companies. It is generally said that these funds represent the savings of the people and therefore should receive special consideration. But investments are placed where returns are high, and generally speaking the higher the returns the higher the risk. Money is not placed on farms from philanthropic motives. Mortgage funds are placed there because in the past the returns have been high. The interest rate on mortgages has run all the way from eight to as high as twelve per cent, nine and ten per cent being the general rule in the early days. A farm mortgage is a commercial venture and should be treated as such. Commercial failures have access to the Bankruptcy Act and to the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act. The farmers should be entitled to similar legislation to suit their special type of business. But the farmer's is the one type of business for which no suitable legislation has been provided by which arrangements may be made to liquidate debts incurred through no fault of his own. A permanent solution, therefore, must be to remove as far as possible the cause of these debts. That is a federal responsibility. Until then suitable debt legislation must be maintained to deal with debt as a recurring problem, and in my view this legislation does not take care of that.

Mr. Speaker, ever since the Supreme Court of Canada declared the debt adjustment legislation of Alberta to be ultra vires, those of us from the west have been most anxious that the federal parliament should pass legislation to give a measure of protection to the farmers of Canada and particularly the farmers of the prairie provinces. The legislation which is now before us is in my opinion a pitiful reply to a crying need for some action in this regard.
The whole question of debt legislation for the prairie farmers is of long duration. It is a problem which has grown over the years. I do not intend to make a long review of the debt situation. I had intended doing so, but in view of the fact that the session is nearing its close and members are naturally anxious to go home, I think it is unnecessary to make a long review of the debt situation, with its cumulative effects piling up over the last thirty or forty years. Suffice it for me to draw

Farmers' Creditors Act

the attention of the house to the submission made on March 15, 1943, to the federal parliament by the western debt conference. That was not a political conference; it was not made up of persons who could by any manner of means be described as radical. It was made up of representatives of the governments of the three prairie provinces, one a liberal government, another a coalition government, and the third a Social Credit government, and representatives of farmers' organizations from the three western provinces. I think that conference represented a fair cross-section of the opinion of western Canada on this debt problem and they placed their views succinctly before the government.
They point out first of all that this debt problem was attributable in part to the rapidity with which land settlement took place in western Canada from 1906 onwards. They point out that most of the equipment and land and buildings were obtained at high prices on borrowed money; that land was purchased at inflation prices; that interest rates were uniformly high, as is characteristic of any pioneer area.
They point out, in the second place, that the ten depression years had their effect on this debt problem, and that the average gross cash income on the prairies from 1926 to 1929 was $537,913,000, while the average corresponding figure from 1930 to 1941 was $260,600,000. They point out that while the index of prices dropped from 100 to 86 in the protected industries, in agriculture it fell from 100 to 48. They also point out that during the drought years, five years and in some parts of Saskatchewan ten years, drought was a contributing factor to debt accumulation and that during that drought period agricultural income in certain areas of the west declined very materially.
Another thing which this debt conference pointed out was that in spite of the fact that
farm prices were better during the war, agricultural income on the prairies for the year 1942 amounted to $462,200,000, and comparing this with the average agricultural income for the three prairie provinces from 1926 to 1929, amounting to $537,913,000, they point out that there is still a deficiency to make up of some $75,000,000 before farm income for the prairie provinces is brought up to that of the average period.

These tables show first of all the interest payable each year on mortgages in each of the provinces of Canada. They show, secondly, the total amount of operating expenses. It will surprise most hon. members to realize that in 1931 28-89 millions of dollars or 38-8 per cent of the operating costs of the Saskatchewan farmer, was interest; in 1936 it was 31 per cent, and in 1937 29-7 per cent. That is a tremendous charge on operating costs. It is even more alarming to find that, as related to the total cash receipts in the province of Saskatchewan, in 1931 41-4 per cent of the farmer's total receipts went to pay interest, 16-5 per cent in 1936, and 23-1 per cent in 1937. I think hon. members will recognize that in a fluctuating economy such as ours in the west, with incomes varying from year to year, and with so large a percentage of the farmer's operating costs and so large a percentage of the total income going to pay interest on mortgages, the problem is a very serious one indeed. That is why all the prairie provinces have been 72537-319}
forced by the pressure of public opinion and by the needs of the situation to pass some debt adjustment legislation.
In 1934 the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed by the dominion parliament, and amendments have since been enacted from time to time. The creditor class of this country have always been opposed to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act; they have done everything in their power to have the scope of its activity limited, and it was limited in 1938, with the result that for some years only the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta came within the benefits of that legislation. As public opinion developed in western Canada and it became more and more apparent that every government in the west was going to pass debt adjustment legislation which would give greater benefits to the debtor class, this legislation was taken to the courts, and last year the Supreme Court of Canada declared the western debt adjustment legislation to be ultra vires. I think it is significant that there
Farmers' Creditors Act

was no question of challenging the validity of that legislation until such time as it became apparent that the pressure of public opinion was going to force that legislation to become more and more useful in the interests of the debtor class. As that became apparent the power has been taken away from the western provinces where the pressure of public opinion in that direction is so strong, and is now to be vested in the dominion parliament.
When it was learned that the matter was to be referred to the dominion parliament, the three prairie provinces joined together for the purpose of making representations to the government, and this they did last summer, last fall, and again this spring. They presented "an act to provide for the adjustment and settlement of debts of farmers." I think it is interesting to notice the difference between that title and the title of the legislation now before the house. The legislation which this house is about to decide upon is "an act to facilitate compromises and arrangements between insolvent farmers and their creditors." It might better have been called "an act for the liquidation of farmers."
It is significant to read the proposed act which was submitted to the federal government by the debt conference and compare it with the legislation which is now before the house. I wish to draw attention to some of the differences in the two pieces of legislation.
First, may I draw attention to the difference in the powers which it was proposed should be given under the debt conference proposal and the powers which are to be given under the legislation before the house at this time. The act recommended by the conference suggested, under a proposed section 9, that-
(1)	Upon application of any farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due, the board shall have the power to formulate a plan of settlement with respect to any debt or debts of the farmer which will, in the opinion of the board, ensure that the farmer will continue to farm the land and be an efficient producer.
(2)	Without derogating from the generality of subsection (1) and regardless of when the debt was incurred or whether the debt is secured or unsecured, the board on formulating the plan of settlement may:
(a) alter the terms of payment of any debt;
. (b) reduce the principal and/or interest of any debt;
(c) reduce the rate of interest on any debt. . .
In the proposed act the powers which were to be given to the board that was to settle and adjust debts are definitely set out. Under the bill now before the house-I shall not read from it, because we will do that in committee-the matter is to be referred to

the courts with power to compose, arrange or extend. This is a serious departure. The board which was set up in 1934, headed by a judge, started out with a judicial aspect on this question, with all the sense of property rights peculiar to the judiciary. The result was that the adjustments in the first few years were pitifully small and inadequate. The government itself recognized that. Later a new board was set up, and as that board went around the country and became familiar with conditions its adjustments became more generous, with the result that some of the adjustments made in recent years have been fair and proper. The reasons to my mind are twofold. First, this was a board which had moved around among the people and become aware of conditions. I personally have listened to cases being heard before them, and that in places where the atmosphere of the neighbourhood would have its influence upon the decision. Second, on that board there would be other than the judiciary and it would be possible for the farmers' representative to present the farmers' point of view. But under this new act the whole matter is to be left to the judge; there will be no farmer representation sitting in, no board which has been able to develop a liberal and sympathetic view over a period of years. I think that the setting up of this court with its limited powers is a retrogressive step.
In the next place I want to point out that under this proposed legislation which was placed before the government there was a provision by which the farmer's equity would be preserved in the event of any adjustment which might take place. In section 15 of the proposed act we find this:
In exercising its jurisdiction and powers and powers to formulate a plan of settlement and without limiting its discretion in any -way the board may consider and determine inter alia the following matters:
(1)	The value of the farmer's interest in the farm lands as represented by the amount of money, principal and interest paid by him to the vendor, mortgagee, encumbrancee, or other creditors in respect of the land, and the amount of cultivation, improvements or labour made or expended by him in bringing the lands to their present productive capacity;
(2)	The ability of the debtor to pay and to that end to arrange the payments of his creditors in such amounts and at such times as the debtor may reasonably be expected to meet, having regard to his present and prospective capability to perform the terms and conditions of the plan and having regard to the productive capacity of his farm;
(3)	The cost of maintenance of the debtor and his family at a reasonable standard of living and the current expenditures reasonably necessary in the operation of his farm.

Farmers' Creditors Act
There are three fundamental principles: (1) that in the adjustment of any debt the farmer's equity shall be preserved and guaranteed; (2) that his ability to pay shall be taken into consideration on the basis of the productive capacity of his land; (3) that the cost of maintenance of himself and his family shall be regarded as one of the vital considerations in making an adjustment. I find nothing like that in the proposed legislation. The whole power put into the hands of the court shows an ingrained sense of property rights, with no provision at all to guarantee that the farmer's interests and his equity shall be maintained.
I call attention to another point, and that is that in the proposed act submitted to the federal government there was a recommendation that would take care of future contingencies. No board and no judge can say to a debtor and a creditor: "Here is a settlement. You, the debtor, will pay to the creditor a certain amount of money per annum. This case is now closed once for all." That cannot be done because such a settlement is based on the assumption that the farmer's crops will continue to materialize and that his income will remain more or less stable. But we know from sad experience in the west that that does not happen. We have had periods of drought and periods of depressed prices, and an adjustment made to-day may be impossible of fulfilment five years from now.
The proposed act placed before the federal government dealt with that contingency. Section 24 provided:
A farmer, in any year in which his income from agriculture together with any other income he may have is not sufficient to meet his liabilities payable in that year as they become due, may apply to the board for directions as to how he shall distribute that income. The board, after allowing for the reasonable needs of his family and the requirements of farm operations until the next harvesting season commences, may direct how his income from all sources shall in that year be applied, and upon the farmer's compliance with these directions, the farmer, notwithstanding any contracts he may have made, shall not in law be regarded as in default with respect to that year's liabilities, and unless with the consent of the board no action or proceeding shall be taken in respect of such liabilities and the farmer's said income shall not be subject to garnishment or attachment or seizure or any legal process.
I submit to the Minister of Finance that the absence of any provision such as that in this bill, or in the regulations which will be issued under the act, will jeopardize the success of this legislation. I refer the minister to a statement which appears in "Prairie Population Possibilities:	A study
prepared for the Royal Commission on
Dominion-Provincial Relations by W. J. Waines." I call the minister's attention to the following, on page 54:
Farm Debt-the need for a more flexible instrument than the Mortgage.
The burden of this rigid interest cost fluctuates greatly from year to year. Since 1928 it has varied from less than a tenth to nearly a third of the total gross cash receipts (8 per cent in 1928, 31 per cent in 1932 and 14 per cent in 1937). It is, however, net operating income, not gross income, out of which interest on debt and the living expenses of the farm family have to be met. Between 1928 and 1932 the share of the net cash operating income taken by interest rose from a tenth to nearly three-quarters. In 1937, after considerable amounts had been written off and interest rates reduced, it still amounted to about one-quarter of net cash operating income. In years of good crops and higher prices, the interest cost can be met relatively easily; in years of low income, resulting either from poor crops, low prices, or a combination of both such as was experienced" during the depression it becomes an almost impossible burden. Defaults and the accumulation of arrears are the ways of escape. Under these circumstances there is a very strong case for the use of a more flexible instrument of farm finance than the mortgage-an instrument which will give the "lender" a proprietary share in the income of the farm enterprise rather than a fixed annual claim against it.
Failure to provide some flexible instrument for future settlements will condemn this legislation before it is many years old.
Let me indicate another serious omission. Subsection 2 of section 18 of the proposed act submitted to the government by the debt conference had this provision:
(a)	Every proposal under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act may be revised by the board upon the application of the debtor within five years of the date of this act coming into force.
(b)	Upon the application of the debtor to revise a plan of settlement made under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. the board shall have the same powers and the revised plans shall be subject to the terms and conditions as if made in the first instance under the provisions of this act.
That was a good suggestion. I do not know that five years is the right length of time; it might be longer or shorter; but if we are to allow for a probationary period during which they could see how the settlement worked out, and if in the first five years it were found impossible to fulfil the conditions and terms of settlement, the creditor could bring his case once more before the board and have some adjustment made. If, however, the plan of settlement operated successfully for five years, they suggested that from there on it should be accepted as a fixed settlement. But they did provide for some probationary period.
I see no provision of that sort here, and I think that is a serious omission. That is
Farmers' Creditors Act

certainly what ruined the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in the early years. Proposals were formulated when those who were formulating them had little or no experience in administering -legislation of the kind. The result was, if I remember rightly, that the average cut in debt was about 16 per cent in the first year or two. That grew in some instances to as high as 47 per cent in later years, because the first boards were timid and were feeling their way. But the fact remains that the people who came before the boards were penalized because they happened to be the first to come under the legislation. The settlement was final. I appreciate the fact that under the new legislation those people who came in prior to 1938 will be able to have their compositions reexamined, but I do suggest to the minister that there should be some provision for a revision of a case in which the debtor finds that the terms of settlement are beyond his powers to fulfil.
One more observation I have to make with reference to this bill. There is a provision of the bill now before the house which does not appear in the proposed legislation placed before the government by the western debt conference. I should like to know who is responsible for it. I refer to the right of appeal to the appeal court. It is no secret that ever since the proposed act to which I refer was placed before the government by the western debt conference a persistent and determined lobby has been carried on throughout this country in editorial columns of the newspapers, and in the form of brochures that have been sent to members of parliament and scattered widespread throughout the country, against the type of legislation proposed by the debt conference and seeking either to prevent any such legislation being passed or so to weaken and dilute it when it did come to the house that it would have little or no value.
In my opinion section 23 of the bill is nothing more or less than a sell-out to the lobby that has been carried on by the creditor class across Canada. Who is going to receive benefits from this provision? Certainly not the debtor class. The people who can best afford to appeal, the people who can best afford to wait, the people who can best afford to go through the legal procedure will always be the mortgage company and the trust company. I think this measure can be condemned on that section alone, because it would appear that the only proposal that w'ill be formulated is the proposal in which the creditor feels he has more than an even break. When he feels that he has not more than an even break, he will put the debtor to fMr. T. C. Douglas.]
all the trouble and expense of taking this matter to the appeal court. No matter to what extent you may try to save him legal expenses by providing legal services, there are other expenses which must be met by a farmer travelling to town when, his case is to be heard. Other trips will have to be made to see other parties; he will have his travelling and living expenses when he has to stay in town a few days while his case is pending. These things may not seem important, but they are important to people who have not much money to travel long distances. Every time,you grant the right of appeal, that is a privilege to a privileged group rather than to the people whom this legislation is supposed to assist.
In my opinion the farmer has become the victim of both ends of the economic process. He has become the victim at the one end because we have failed to give him parity prices for his products, and at the other end we have failed to give him adequate protection against the loss of his home. All that this bill proposes to do is to provide debt postponement. It is not a solution; it is simply debt postponement which will put off the day of reckoning so that the farmer may be kept on the farm -as a producer and as one upon whom the creditor class may levy a tribute. But in the way of solution by removing the debt, in the way of reinstating a farmer on his farm as the owner or operator of that farm, there is nothing in this measure to provide for that. I agree with the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when he says that if the government established a system of parity prices and crop insurance for the farmer we would not need debt legislation, because the farmer could take care of himself. I maintain that as long as the government is going to continue to make the farmer the orphan or the stepchild of our economy, he has a right to expect legislation which will not -merely postpone the day of reckoning but which will deal with the fundamental problem of debt. I fail to see anything of that nature in this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the very important part which the farmer plays in our economy entitles him to any adjustment of debt which was incurred during those difficult times known as the depression. Reference has been made to the conference held by the three prairie provincial governments. I propose to take only a few minutes to make some general remarks, and then when the bill is in committee I shall probably ask a few questions with respect to some of the sections. I think the proposals put forward by this conference should have

Farmers' Creditors Act
received a little more consideration, because they represented the general opinion, not only of the farmer of western Canada but of the merchant and the other classes which are dependent upon the success of the farmer.
I do not think it is necessary to give any figures with respect to farmer debt or the portion the farmer receives of our national income, because these figures have been placed before the house on many occasions. I think we are all agreed that the farmer should receive a little larger share of the national income. It is generally recognized that there must be some means of adjustment by which the farmer may be taken out of his debt difficulty. All we want is something that is fair. When we consider this bill we realize that it will mean bankruptcy to many farmers. They might just as well go bankrupt and be done with it. I admit that a number of reasonable adjustments have been made under the previous aot, but that was due to a great extent to the fact that the farmers had representation on the board of review; that the proposals were made by someone representing the farmers and who had had personal experience in farming and knew the difficulties under which agriculture was being carried on.
As the previous speaker (Mr. Douglas) has said, this bill substitutes a district court for the board of review when the creditor and debtor cannot come to an agreement. There is an appeal to the appeal court. I think there must be some final appeal, and there is no question that it should be to a court. Debts incurred prior to 1935 are really in a special class. They were incurred during the previous ten years, or at least during the previous eight or nine years when farmers were passing through a most difficult period. This bill provides that if in making a proposal two-thirds of the debt has been contracted prior to 1935 and is taken into consideration in the proposal, then they will consider all debt up to the present time. I think that is good as far as it goes, but some special consideration should be given to this debt, or there ought to be some means of handling debts contracted prior to 1935 because they are in a different class.
There are one or two principles in the bill with which I cannot agree. One is that the farmer cannot sell his farm within five years after a proposal has been made; if he happens to find a purchaser he cannot sell without the approval of the receiver. Also he cannot sell any of the products from his farm unless he accounts to the receiver. Therefore he is practically in the hands of the receiver in regard to selling any of his farm products.
The rate of interest is dealt with at page 14 of the bill, and I feel that this section must be revised and a lower rate substituted.
I want to make a plea also for those in the west who are operating farms though not residing on them. Many men who have retired, either because of age or as a result of physical disability, are living in towns but are still operating their farms, and the definition of a resident farmer should be cleared up. As I understand the bill, a man must actually reside on the farm. I recall that in 1934, when the first Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was being considered, I made a special plea on behalf of these people and received quite a good deal of support from various hon. members of the house. Men who, though not residing on the farm, pay all the expenses, own the machinery and have to meet the debts incurred in previous years, cannot take advantage of this bill, as I understand it, and they should be given some consideration.
The bill also provides that no farmer shall be entitled to make more than one proposal, and I believe that provision should be repealed. As I have said, I am not going to take much time in this debate; I desired to speak generally just for a moment or two. However, I have received some letters in this connection, one of which I have in my hand, coming from the council at Balgonie, in Saskatchewan, asking me to make certain representations in regard to the interest rate, which I have done. These letters, I may say, were written before the bill was printed. They also suggest that applications be accepted from executors, which I think is provided in the bill, and they think the farmer should be permitted to make^ a second proposal. These letters also mention one or two further suggestions which I do not think are quite reasonable; therefore I am not presenting them at the moment, though I may do so at another stage. All I have to say now is that I hope the minister will give consideration to amending some provisions of the bill as we go through it in committee.

We have waited quite a long time for the bill now before the house, and I must say that I am just as much disappointed in it as any of the hon. members who have already spoken. Being one of the victims of circumstances over which I had no control, I feel that I might give a few instances that would be of interest to the house. I started in western Canada in 1914, working on a farm to get experience while somebody else
Farmers' Creditors Act

got the profits. I worked on that farm during 1914 and 1915. In 1916 I started on my own, and during 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919 I did
not thresh as much grain as I had put into the ground for seed. That was the start I had as a practical farmer; and over that period1 I had to work at anything and everything I could get to do in order to pay the interest on the money I owed. Needless to say I was much further in debt at the end of that four-year period than I was when I began, though I had put in four hard years and somebody else had reaped the benefit.
I do not think there is any particular need for me or anyone else to waste much time in telling of the trials and tribulations through which the farmers have gone, because the representatives of the three western provinces laid their case plainly before the government, backed by all kinds of statistics. But we find that another group has been to the government and presented its case, and from the make-up of the present bill I feel that this group must be the power behind the scene. The farmer is being used to produce, and somebody else reaps the profits. From my own experience I can truthfully say that if I had not worked at anything and everything I could get to do outside of the farm, I would have been on the road many years ago. However, I built up the most economical farm unit I could; I made use of every bit of help I hired. I woi^ced every hour I could, more than once going for thirty-six hours without sleep, and I am still on the farm; but if it had not been for money I earned in other work I would have been on the road with hundreds of others who have had that unpleasant experience during the years I have been in Canada.
When I was home on my last visit, just before getting on the train to return to Ottawa a farmer told me his latest experience with the mortgage companies. He had obtained a loan of $9,500 on his land and buildings; he had paid back $6,500 and made improvements to his farm worth $1,200, but finally was forced on the road. To show that land values change very drastically, immediately after this farmer was put on the road, his farm was sold for $2,400, though some time previously he had been able to get a loan of $9,500 on it. Only this morning I received a letter from a soldier settler who has been served with thirty days' notice to vacate. He gives a little of his history, and then says:
Following the 1929 crop failure, I was clear of debt in the spring of 1930 and had $600 cash. Although I had five thousand bushels of wheat that year. . . .

I know the district in which this man resides, and I know there was a crop failure in 1929.
... I went $1,500 in the hole on the crop; 174 cents for wheat, 9 cents for threshing, 5 cents for hauling, leaving 3J cents for all other expenses. Before I got over that I had lost a new' binder and a threshing outfit I had bought, and the years of low prices which follow'ed, combined with the outside wrork I had to do to keep the farm running at all, broke my heart and I was in hospitals and bed for two years and couldn't u'ork for tw'o more. But I am just naturally optimistic. This spring I went to work against doctor's orders and I put in 250 acres of crop with very little help. And although I am played out right now I think I will get over it in time for harvest.
This is only one of the instances which could be cited to show the adverse conditions through which the farmers have been passing.
I	remember distinctly that in 1930 on my own farm I threshed 10,600 bushels of wheat and over 5,000 bushels of oats. The wheat averaged me 121 cents a bushel, and it cost
II	cents a bushel to thresh. I believe we paid 7 cents for threshing the oats, and sold them for 14 cents. While those things were happening I continued to pay eight per cent interest, and nothing was said about it. A number of other farmers were paying exactly the same rate. The bill before the house to-day is one of the results of the policy carried on at that time, and the condition then allowed to develop.
While we were getting those prices for our grain and other farm produce, when we were selling hogs for two cents a pound, eggs for three cents a dozen and butterfat for nine cents a pound, when we were receiving prices of that kind for our products, the price of our farm machinery climbed every year, with one exception. In that year there was a reduction of about $5 in each implement we had to buy. So that I do not feel that the bill introduced to-day goes far enough. At present we have a ban on communism, and unless something is done perhaps we will need one or two other bans in the very near future; because from the way farmers are being treated to-day, and have been in the past, there is no possibility of their getting out of debt. When the farmer is compelled to produce below the cost of production, and pay up principal and interest on debts accumulated some time ago, during depression and previous years, there is no possibility whatever of his getting out of the hole, despite the fact that he works 150 per cent of the time worked by other labourers in Canada. Before farmers can even begin to put their house in order they will have to have an equitable debt adjustment act. In addition we must have parity prices
