Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a -few words respecting the general principles of the bill introduced a few days ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). The measure is a new one, but it seems to me it follows closely the previous act known as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. This it seems to me is a desirable feature in that the principles of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, so far as it was applicable in the different provinces of Canada, are reasonably well understood. Under these circumstances the machinery of the organization now to be set up will also be understood before it begins to operate. The fact that people are familiar with the operation of the old act will assist in the operation of the new one when it becomes effective.
I do not think any useful purpose would be served at this time in going over the history of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and what has happened in connection with its operation, particularly as it has affected different sections of Canada. When that act was first introduced it was applicable to all of Canada. At different periods, from then on, action was taken by which various provinces were removed from the application of the act, and eventually it reached the point where it was applicable only to the three western provinces. In 1938 its operation in Manitoba was discontinued. That, however, was not because of any action on the part of the House of Commons, but because of one particular feature which has been attended to in the present measure.
The new legislation differs from the old in that it provides a change in the machinery of administration from the principle of using official receivers and boards of review to that of using county clerks and the judiciary. So far as I am concerned, I am bound to say I would much prefer to a continuance of the use of official receivers. I believe official receivers, when carefully selected, would have a different approach to the matter than would many of the county court clerks. Moreover, as I understand the set-up of judicial districts, 72537-320
particularly those in western Canada, they cover large areas. So that if there is to be only one county court clerk in a judicial district, to act as an official receiver, it will cause great inconvenience to many farmers who would have to reach a particular centre to make application under this measure. I submit therefore that that particular feature of the machinery should have further consideration. I understand that for certain purposes provision is made for additional appointments; but I submit that in this particular regard judicial districts are too large for administrative purposes, and particularly for farmers wishing to have their cases in order.
The other change in the measure, having to do with the arrangements for appeal, presents the difficulty which developed when the old act was under consideration, and particularly when it was considered in another part of this building. There should not be any objection to the right of appeal. It has many things in its favour, and while some may believe that to some extent it is a hardship on the farmer to have him subjected to further appeals in that regard, yet it has the advantage of at least assuring greater uniformity. So far as additional costs are concerned, as I understand the provisions of the measure such costs need not be charged up against the farmer. It is more likely that they will be charged against the mortgage company or the creditor who will exercise the right of appeal. So that I do not believe the farmer's position is prejudiced to any great extent in that regard.
The other change appearing in the new measure which is of great importance to Manitoba is the provision through which that province may be brought within the scope of the act, along with Saskatchewan and Alberta. This has been one of the controversies among farmers in Manitoba for some time. They claim, and with sound grounds I believe, that Manitoba has just as much entitlement to the provisions of the act as the other two western provinces. We are therefore gratified to see that this measure is made applicable to Manitoba.
Like the earlier legislation, the principle of the measure is founded upon the idea that the efficient farmer shall be maintained on the land. It might be just as well, when we are considering the bill, to refer to some of the declarations that were made when the act was under consideration in the session of 1938. Following some observations I had made at that time, Mr. Bennett used these words:
It was predicated upon two considerations. The first was that it was desirable to keep the farmers on the land. That was part of the

Farmers' Creditors Act

preamble of the act, that they should be retained in possession of their farms. The second was that inasmuch as under section 7 of the Bankruptcy Act a farmer could not take advantage of the provisions of that statute, we should without making him bankrupt give him all the benefits which would accrue if he were able to take advantage of that statute.
Later on the same hon. gentleman used these words:
Just as soon as it was apparent that this legislation was on the statute books, these voluntary arrangements became the order of the day. As soon as it was apparent that by voluntary effort and cooperation these arrangements could be carried out, when the extent to *which the statute went was not generally known, these settlements were made.
That is a principle of this legislation which I think it is desirable to have in mind and which I, and I think many of us, hoped would be the scope of legislation by which voluntary settlements could be arranged and then given the force of law. We have had experience in the past of voluntary arrangements being made with no provision for bringing them into effect by law, and occasionally difficulties arose with respect to them later. But with this machinery many settlements may be effected and given final approval by the court.
I recall the discussions when the previous act was under consideration. One of the things that stood out at that time was the circumstances of a farmer who had placed a mortgage on his farm and then ran into a certain amount of difficulty and found himself unable to keep up his payments, which got further and further behind until the burden became altogether too great for him to carry. We have all seen cases where the mortgage company or whoever had a financial claim on the property exercised the right of foreclosure and obliged the farmer to leave what was virtually his homestead property, the home to which he had become attached during his lifetime, the home that had a great deal of sentimental value for him, and in so many cases we have seen that farm which the farmer was forced to leave resold to someone else at a lower valuation. When one considers the sentimental attachment one has for his home, it is a pretty hard thing for anyone to be uprooted from the place where he has been living a lifetime and then see the property turned over to someone else at a lower price than that at which it would be given to him to enable him to carry on. Machinery of this kind can take care of such cases.
So far as Manitoba is concerned, I confess that from a factual point of view I am not in a position to say to what extent the legislation is required or is desirable or necessary. We have had in our province, as in the other
[Mr. Weir.l
provinces, provincial debt adjustment boards which have had a very considerable effect. They have, however, no authority, and it was not intended that they should have authority, to compel adjustments except to a limited degree. But they did have the effect of taking care to a very considerable extent of conditions that were to say the least provoking and pressing. In the main that is a very satisfactory type of legislation, particularly if it could be understood that it would be adhered to. But in view of court decisions with respect to the Alberta legislation the general feeling in Manitoba is that it is only a matter of time before our provincial debt adjustment legislation will be challenged and declared ultra vires, and then we shall have no debt adjustment machinery and no machinery at all for controlling the debt situation in Manitoba. We are therefore very anxious that some machinery shall be set up to take care of the debt situation among the farmers of that province, if for no other reason than the possibility of the provincial debt legislation being discarded. The legislation is supported, perhaps not in exactly this form, by the provincial government which joined with the western debt conference in representations to the federal government for legislation, perhaps not exactly like what we have before us, but in principle something akin to it. The federation of agriculture in the province of Manitoba has also been strong in its advocacy of debt adjustment legislation.

Through a series of dry years he found it impossible to meet his obligations, and at the same time he was compelled to reduce the number of his live stock considerably, until finally he found himself in such difficulty that he was obliged to give up his farm before it was foreclosed.

I mentioned a while ago that we have a provincial debt adjustment board in Manitoba. It has done very good work and has been of real benefit to the farmers who were having difficulties in financing their operations. I have not a full record of what they have accomplished since the Manitoba debt adjustment act was enacted, but I have before me a summary of the operations of the board for the past two years. In the year 1941 the board dealt with 315 mortgage cases, 59 agreements of sale, and 784 tax sale applications, a total of 1,149 cases, in which certificates were requested to take foreclosure proceedings but were refused. In 1942, 333 mortgage cases were dealt with, 103 agreements of sale, and 588 tax sale applications, a total of 1,024 farm cases where certificates were refused. All the board was able to do in these cases was to refuse a certificate to allow a sale, whether it was a tax sale, or foreclosure proceedings were to be instituted. In addition to that the board has been able to effect many compromises and agreements with the creditor class. In all, with the cases dealt with by them over a two-year period, they claim to have effected, in principal and interest by mutual arrangement, reductions to the extent of $444,000. So that while some may argue, and I suppose they will, that Manitoba, having got along without this debt adjustment legislation for some time, can continue to do without it, that is not the case; I contend that Manitoba is just as much entitled to legislation of this kind as are the other western provinces.

Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battleford): I do not wish to take up the time of the house in repeating what has been said, but I should like to support entirely what has been said by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas).

It may appear to the minister and to the government that the type of legislation which they are bringing down at this time fulfils a certain need, but that if a longer range view is taken of this question it will be found that you are destroying the fundamental faith of our people in the land. We in Canada have always considered that agriculture is our basic industry, that it supports large numbers of people, and that the general prosperity of the country depends to a very great degree upon that foundation of our agricultural popu-iation. I know that in the future we are going to become a far greater industrial country, but still there is a future also for the vast prairies and the people w'ho live on them.
I have received much correspondence on this question and it seems to be always the same type of complaint more or less that is voiced. Only on June 30, from someone living in my own part of the country, I

received the following letter. My correspondent ' is a w'oman. After a few introductory remarks she says:
We have just received a summons from the Saskatchewan farm loan board re foreclosure on our homestead filed thirty years ago in 1913. There is no need to tell you what we have gone through these last years-depression and relief. Of course, payments were not made and interest accumulated. We began on this land with four children and no cash at all. We were glad to work out to keep the family, and have worked on the land with the time we have had left. Together we have raised fourteen children. We have one hundred acres broken now and we are going to lose all that and the work we have done through the years, because the years were lean and the crops failed. There does not seem to be much relation between a thing like this ahd the words spoken in mid-Atlantic by those two men. Churchill and Roosevelt-that all men should have the privilege of living their lives in freedom from fear and want. Do you know what will happen to this land of ours? It will be sold for a hundred dollars or so to land-grabbers who happen to have the ready cash. It has been done in three instances. One farm was sold for $25, another for $75 and a halfsection, nearly all broken, for $400. But we who have done all the work-not a penny will be left for us. We have to pay in full or lose our land.
This courageous couple who raised fourteen children are going to make a start now in their old age in a new part of the country and build a new home for themselves. It seems to me that rural children and the farm people have supplied, and will continue to supply, and continue to be the reservoir for the supply of many fine citizens to this nation. But in the bill we have before us at the present time we are destroying the faith of the people in their ability to live and make and maintain a home on the land. This particular couple raised fourteen children- what a contribution to Canada that in itself was. We say we want more Canadian-born people in Canada-Canada for Canadians; but is this any encouragement to people to raise large families? In the future our fariji people will not go in for large families. If this couple had not had fourteen children they might have been able to get along better, to maintain themselves and keep their home. everything is gone.
I cannot help feeling that the scheme embodied in this bill, although in a short-range view it may appear to satisfy the needs of the moment, will be found in the long run to be one of the most disastrous measures brought into effect for the rural people of Canada.

I rise to make a few observations on the proposed debt act now before the house. The farmers of Canada, I am sure, have been waiting with a great deal of impatience for the federal government to pass adequate debt legislation which would once and for all time solve their debt problems and offer them some means of protection. But as we see it this afternoon, and judging by the bill which has been brought in, the proposed legislation was drafted not for the protection of our farmers but for the protection of the interests of finance. I should like to make that statement as plain as I possibly can, because members who come from western Canada have to deal with a great number of debt cases. It is almost impossible for one to realize that farmers, who have given their best to the upbuilding of Canada, are finally thrown out on the road. The people of western Canada in particular will be greatly disappointed that the government did not see fit to bring in a measure which would adequately take care of the debt situation in Canada for all time.
It seems futile to argue with the minister or with the government or to point out that this debt legislation falls far short of what our people were expecting and to what they are entitled. The government seems to follow a traditional policy of ignoring the pleas and the demands of the farmers. Let me read a short clipping from the Calgary Albertan of May, 14, 1943. I believe it will throw light on the subject:
Farmer Evicted. Gaoled. Goods, Family, Left on Road
Edmonton, May 13.-Edwin Broder, 51-year-old farmer of Edmonton went to gaol for seven days to-day at the order of Police Magistrate A. I. Millar on conviction of a charge of obstructing eviction proceedings which left his furniture piled on a public highway and his wife and eight children without a home. The eviction order was made in the supreme court. The evidence indicated Broder tried to stop the sheriff's bailiff from carrying it out. "You had been told to get out?" asked the magistrate. "Yes," replied Broder, "but no one likes to lose his home. He will stay as long as he can." "The supreme court must have had a good reason for issuing the order," said Mr. Millar. "There may have been a reason and there may not have been a reason," the farmer answered. "I bought a quarter section of land for $4,800 on time in 1916. I raised a family of eight children, paid the owner of the land $5,600, and I still owe $5,600. I had to go through the depression years and I was hailed out a year ago." Neither Broder nor the court disclosed the circumstances surrounding the eviction order. Meanwhile the farmer's wife and family were taken in to be cared for by neighbours.
That is the sort of thing we have to contend with in the prairie provinces. The proposed
act brought in by the minister is not good enough. It may have been a good start ten years ago, but to-day, after our farmers have been struggling for more than ten years under the most adverse circumstances, it is not good enough to bring in a measure of this sort, which does not contain a single recommendation made by the farm debt conference. Let me ask the minister this question. If he is not going to listen to our farmers and accept their suggestions, whose suggestions is he going to consider? When dealing with farm debt or with farm problems the government should take the advice of members of our agricultural communities and farm organizations. This idea of forcing anything at all upon our farmers, whether they like it or not, is entirely out of date. I am certain the farmers will not receive this bill with any hope or encouragement.
At this time, more than ever before, the farmers of Canada are expected to produce more than ever before. This they must do with depleted machinery, shortage of labour, and having to pay high prices for everything they buy. Whatever he may get in return, even though fair prices are being paid for a number of commodities, the average farmer in western Canada is still not in a position to carry on and pay off his debts. It is pitiful that, while farmers' sons are serving this country overseas, the financial institutions are taking advantage of the situation and are foreclosing upon farmers by thousands. It is most unfair.
The suggestion has been made both in the press and in this house that there are farmers who are inefficient. Anyone who dares to call our farmers inefficient, I do not care who he is, does not know what he is talking about. The farmers of Canada have produced all the foodstuffs that were required, and they are producing all that is required to-day. They are carrying their burden nobly and at great sacrifice. Yet some men even dare to suggest that there are inefficient farmers. Surely the farmers have never failed this country. For many years they were placed in such a position that they could hardly exist, and this would discourage anyone from continuing to- produce without a fair return to which one is entitled.
I have clippings here which show that the farmers of Canada have done their best to meet their debt obligations. The Globe and Mail of May 9, 1942, contains an article by Mr. Wellington Jeffers, financial editor, which reads:
Farmers in both the United States and Canada have been paying off their farm debt as a result of better prices received during the war. The figures are not available, but insurance men who have this situation always under
Farmers' Creditors Act

their eyes report that a considerable effort has been made in the last three years by farmers. Even in Alberta, in spite of moratoria, farmers have been coming forward of their own free will and paying what they owed whenever they could.
That is a fair indication of farmers' willingness to pay their debts. I maintain that whenever the farmer has undertaken a debt obligation he has done his best to meet it. I have here another clipping from that great Canadian daily which has always stood for the farmer and for adequate debt adjustment, the Edmonton Bulletin. Mr. Harold L. Weir, one of the editors of that paper, had this to say on March 4, 1942:
Since the year 1930, the farmers of this province have encountered a series of misfortunes, due to no fault of their own, which have now culminated in a situation which virtually amounts to their economic disinheritance.
Further down it says:
At last the Bennett government brought in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act with the purpose of so adjusting the farmer's debts that the farmer could remain on the land in the public interest as a free man and not as a serf.
Everyone hailed this piece of legislation as a measure of vital interest to the farmers and to the country at large which depended upon agricultural prosperity to promote and assure its own welfare.
What has happened to this act which was designed to rescue the farmer from economic oblivion? What has been its effect in this province?
Well, the Alberta board of review started in to make adjustments and cut interest rates on loans down to seven per cent. Later on, adjustments were made with interest rates at six per cent until, finally, Chief Justice C. R. Mitchell, chairman of the Alberta board of review, announced that all future adjustments would carry interest at no more than five per cent.
It would be interesting to the public to know exactly how these adjustments are made.
The board first adds up all the farmer's liabilities, which, let us assume for the sake of example, total $7,500.
The board's inspector next evaluates the farmer's assets-his land and equipment and improvements-which, for instance, may amount to $5,000.
The board then wipes off $2,500 of the farmer's liabilities so that these may not exceed his assets. In short, the act generously provides that a man need not owe more than the value of %vhat he owns.
But the farmer, under this adjustment, must pay five per cent interest on the newly established value of his assets and since his liabilities are fixed at exactly the same level as his assets, he is not left one dollar of equity in those assets.
The adjustment may appear to be fair on the face of it. But when the farmer is required to meet his living expenses, to pay taxes and attempt to carry out the terms of the adjustment with five per cent interest, he inevitably finds that, owing to the price of his products being below cost of production, he cannot possibly meet the terms laid down by the board.
[Mr. Hlynka.l
The vast majority of more than 200,000 farmers living in the three western provinces, in spite of all the adjustments, find themselves economic slaves with no possible chance under present conditions of ever getting out of debt.
This indicates the almost hopeless situation in which a great many of our farmers in western Canada find themselves.
May I quote one more reference which appeared in the Edmonton Bulletin, the champion of the farmer, on a front page editorial on August S, 1938:
The farmers and, home owners of Alberta have been ruthlessly exploited by the highest interest rates charged anywhere in the British commonwealth of nations. Usury at seven, eight, nine, ten and1 up fo fourteen per cent has been the rule during the entire history of Alberta.
That such interest rates are legal under our laws does not alter the fact that the people of Alberta have been and are being systematically robbed by a small but powerful group of financiers in private control of Canada's monetary system.
Farm loans in the United States are on a long term basis of twenty to thirty years with interest rates of three to three and a half per cent. Home owners pay three and a half to five per cent.
This is another indication of the situation which exists in western Canada. Our munition manufacturers and others received subsidies from this government to enable them to produce with the greatest possible speed and in great volume, but no such subsidies have been given to our farmers. Some may say that many farmers received the acreage bonus, and what not. That was not enough to buy salt for their ham and eggs. Most of that money had been used up in administrative costs, and the farmers received very little. Almost all industries receive support and subsidies from the government; why not place the farmer on the same basis? Then there will be no objection to paying off outstanding debts; for if the farmers were in a position to pay off their debts, they certainly would do so. We all know that incomes of our farmers during the ten year period from 1929 to 1939 were so disgracefully low that it was absolutely impossible for any man, no matter how honest he might have been, to meet his debt obligations and carry on. Listen to what Mr. Jeffers has to say in an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 8, 1943:
The census of 1941 shows that the farmers and farming in Canada are in nothing like the parlous state which might have been expected from recent propaganda at Ottawa from those who want farm credit arrangement acts stiffened in the prairie provinces, and measures taken to forgive a great deal of the debt that already exists.
He goes on to point out that there has been a decrease in farm debt, as follows: in

Farmers' Creditors Act
New Brunswick, by 7-6 per cent; in Ontario, by 14-8 per cent; in Manitoba, by 22-1 per cent; in Saskatchewan, by 6-3 per cent; in Alberta, by 5-3 per cent and in British Columbia by 14 per cent. That decrease took place during the ten year period from 1931 to 1941. In the province of Prince Edward Island there was an increase in farm debt amounting to 22-8 per cent; in Nova Scotia an increase of one per cent and in Quebec an increase of 19 per cent. It may be all right to quote these figures, but the writer of the article overlooks the fact that the decreases he mentions have resulted largely from so many farmers being dispossessed of their land.
I am sorry I do not possess strong enough language adequately to condemn this bill. In time of war, when the farmers have sent their sons to offer their very lives for this country, there is no reason why the government should not give at least adequate protection to agriculture, our basic industry. Were it not for agriculture where would we be?	The majority of our people are
dependent upon agriculture for their very livelihood; yet we listen to complaints by members of the opposition with perhaps only a yawn from the government, and the ministers say nothing when cases are recited about people being dispossessed of their land and that they are losing their life-earnings. Surely it is time even for this reactionary government-which is perhaps the most reactionary government in the history of Canada-to see to it that no farmer is thrown off his land. Why not come out and propose a complete cancellation of interest on all debts until the end of the war and one year after? Why not propose the cancellation of compound interest, which after all is nothing more than a penalty for failure to meet a debt obligation, though we have recognized that it is through no fault of the farmer that he has not paid his debts on time? If it is not his fault, why then should we ask him to suffer this penalty? Nothing has been said about farm credit, which should be extended to farmers on easy terms; for unless the farmer has this credit he cannot meet his debt obligations.
I have only a further word to say. To my mind the most important problem facing the farmers of western Canada to-day is the question of tenancy. If you examine the latest figures available you will find that less than half our farmers own their own homes. Surely they are entitled to a more serious consideration than that. It would be a most dangerous thing that can befall this
nation if we permit our people to lose equity in their homes, which it took perhaps all their lives to build up. Yet we give them only the consideration of referring them to the courts. Well, the house heard what happened to the man about whom I have been quoting. That is what is going to happen to others, unless the minister andi the government take advice from farm organizations in the future. I appeal to the minister even at this late date to revise the whole measure, and to place it on a basis which will include some of the recommendations placed before the minister a few months ago by the farm debt conference.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the farmer in this instance may be compared to a swimmer who is out of his depth and is drowning, with a millstone tied around his neck, and is looking to the House of Commons for assistance. He finds that instead of legislation being introduced which will relieve him of his difficulty, the minister is making arrangements for a pulmotor, or even for the funeral in the event of the body being recovered from the water.
This is a measure to facilitate compromises and arrangements between insolvent farmers and their creditors. Why wait until a farmer is insolvent? Why not do something before he becomes insolvent? I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) could visit some of the debt-ridden farmers in my province and listen to their comments respecting this type of legislation. They know perfectly well it was in a period of high prices that they incurred much of the debt now loaded upon them. They incurred that debt during the last war, and when prices fell they found they could not meet their obligations. When another war loomed up there was the possibility that they might again be able to get some of the high prices they had obtained before. But the minister who is piloting this bill through the house is the man whose legislation has put the ceiling on prices. I am not saying that that is all bad; but I do say it is one thing which has prevented the farmer from paying his debts. Since the government saw fit to interfere at that time and to introduce legislation which has prevented the farmer from paying his debts, then that same government ought to give him more consideration than is being given under this measure in respect of his indebtedness. Particularly is that so in respect of conditions now existing in western Canada, where grain-growers are finding so much difficulty in obtaining cash with which to pay their debts.
Farmers' Creditors Act

The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), who is now in his seat, knows perfectly well that farmers were not allowed to deliver their grain, because he says facilities were not available for taking that grain out of the country, nor was there room in the elevators to store it. But it was cash from that grain which the farmers must use to pay their indebtedness and the interest thereon. The farmer produced the grain, but he could not possibly sell or deliver it. Did the government take steps to see that no interest was piled on farmers' indebtedness during that period? No. Did the government do as was done in the United States? Did it say to the farmers^ "We will give you an advance on the grain which you have properly stored on your farms", so that the farmer could make interest payments? No. That was done in the United States. On the basis of the security of the grain stored on farms the United States government is advancing this year an amount equal to $1.22 No. 1 northern wheat. Even when the farmer is allowed to deliver his wheat in western Canada the ceiling price is only 90 cents Fort William.
Sometimes we hear it said': "Oh, the farmer has other products." Yes, he could turn his grain into cattle, hogs and dairy products. But again this government has prevented! his earning money in that way, particularly in Saskatchewan where the national selective service board, an instrument of this government, has in some instances taken the last boy off the farm. The records prove that Saskatchewan has been badly hit in that way.
A study of the debt problem illustrates some of the basic injustices of the whole economic system under which we operate. Debt is the natural result of the capitalistic system. Under this system the reward to capital always comes first, and the reward to labour is left to take care of itself. It is not recognized. Under this system Shylock demands his pound of flesh-
" the law allows it and the court awards it." The last dollar of production is taken off the farm, whether the mother needs medical attention or the children need clothes. There should be some law in the land establishing a basic income for all families. The mortgage contract is the machination of those who have been given the power to extract the last dollar a man may earn. It has no basis in justice, in humanity or in fairness. If this bill contained the proper provisions it would be an effective agent in restoring the equity of the farmer on his farm and would guarantee to him that so long as he worked his farm well he would have the right to live in security so far as his farm [Mr. CastledenJ
debt was concerned. This bill does not touch that problem at all, and I believe the minister will admit that that, is so.
Farm debt, may I say to the minister, is a national problem from coast to coast. I have been in farming communities in eight of the nine provinces of Canada, and I find the same story told everywhere. If the government does not initiate some legislation to remedy this injustice, some day it will have to make way for a government which will do it. Democracy will not permit that state of affairs to continue much longer.
I shall never forget the story told by a medical doctor at a convention in Saskatchewan some years ago. He had to tell a mother that she was dying of cancer. He said, " Why did you not have this condition cared for a few years ago?" She replied, "I remember your telling me I needed the attention, but that year we had a short crop. We did have some return, but the mortgage company took it all. The next year the children needed clothing and I put it off again. The next year the mortgage company came along and took practically everything we had." "Well," the doctor said, "your three years' delay has cost you your life." If a farmer, his wife and family, labour all year and through no fault of their own have no return, either because of price, because he is not allowed to sell his commodity, or because of drought, rust, hail or storm, surely that man has lost sufficient for one year. Why should a mortgage company suoplying the capital required on a farm always be guaranteed a crop, irrespective of whether the farmer gets a crop or not? Surely this is basically wrong; surely it is something which must be changed. Instead of taking care of the farmer, instead of giving him some assurance that compound interest will not be piled up, instead of ensuring him that the interest in a bad year will be taken care of in some other way, the farmer is further penalized by having interest piled on him as a load of debt. Then the next year the interest is loaded on that of the year before, and interest is piled upon interest, the debt rising and rising until the farmer cannot find his way out.
There are some who say debt adjustment is not necessary. " Why," they say, " the agriculturist is in the best position he ever had." The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven) shouted across the floor to me one evening that the farmers in my district were better off than they ever had been. I have here the quarterly bulletin of agricultural statistics, and at page 200 I find that the total cash income from the sale of farm products from January

Farmers' Creditors Act
to June, 1942, as compared with the same period in 1941 decreased by 23 per cent. In spite of the fact that 1942 was one of the greatest years for the production of farm products, particularly in the west, the province of Saskatchewan shows the lowest increase in cash income of any province in the dominion, the increase in 1942 over 1940 being about twenty-five per cent, while in one other province it went as high as seventy-three per cent.
I know the argument which will be put forward by those who oppose this measure. They will say:	You have to take care of
credit and think of the widows and orphans who have put out their money in farm mortgages. I have examined some twenty cases taken at random, and I find that in only three of them was the farm mortgage held by private individuals, and that in every one of these cases where the creditor was an individual, an ordinary human being like the farmer who is working on the land, they recognized that there was such a thing as justice and made no injurious demand. But in the rest of the cases, where a mortgage or trust company were the creditors, that is where the injustice occurred.
The basis of the tremendous farm debt of the western provinces was the ten years of depression through which they went. The drought in those years should have been recognized as a national calamity, and national measures should have been taken to cope with it. There is no reason why debt should have been allowed to pile up in that period year after year. Surely the farmer suffered enough in those dried-out areas in those cropless years without having to have everything taken away from them, with no relief provided for them with regard to their debt.
Some people may say:	If you adjust farm
debt, you will destroy farm credit. Well, it could not be hurt very much more than it is under the present system. If proper measures had been taken by the federal government the farmers would have paid off every cent of this Shylock-like indebtedness. We need an entirely new set-up with regard to farm credit, and federal funds should be available to agriculture on a production basis.
The farmers will pay their debts if they can. I have known farmers who have done without the necessities of life, gone without food and medical attention, and many of the things that ordinary people consider absolutely necessary, and starved their families, in order to pay interest. I have seen too many hundreds of good farmers lose their whole life's earnings
for anyone to tell me that there is no need of debt legislation-and I do not mean bankrupt legislation.
Some people say: Leave the debt problem alone and it will work itself out. But notice this. As long as money is easy, prices are high and the farmers go into debt. As soon as money is tight, prices are low. A farmer goes into debt when wheat is worth $2 a bushel, as it was in the last war. A debt of $2,000 then means 1,000 bushels of grain to pay it off; but when grain goes down to 40 cents a bushel, to pay off his debt the farmer has to pay back 5,000 bushels of grain. There are, admittedly, some farmers who perhaps extended a little too much and who may not have been quite as saving as they should have been. But you do not need to talk about saving to the farmers of western Canada. They have saved and scrimped far more than anyone should have to do in this land of plenty. I know farmers in the west like the one who borrowed $8,000 and paid back $10,500. This particular farmer wrote to the lending company and asked, "How much do I owe now?" He got the reply "We will settle for $7,500." A friend of mine borrowed $1,700. He paid back $2,100 and I said to him, "You must be paid off now." He said, "Pretty nearly. Ah I owe now js $2,600." In the Prime Minister's constituency last fall I talked to a group of farmers and asked one how he was getting along. He said, "This is a great country. I came here thirty years ago and took a half-section of land all covered with bush, but there was no mortgage. To-day it is all covered with mortgage but no bush on it."
A debt conference of the western provinces was called which asked this government to do something to remedy the debt situation. But this legislation does not even recognize the basic causes of debt. Somebody has said something about the operation of the old act. If you study the figures, you will find that at the rate we are going, the act which has so far covered about 2J per cent of the indebted farmers during each year of its operation, will take forty years to get them all dealt with, and there will be a new crop of debtors by that time.
I have attended the sittings of some of these boards, and the kind of thing I have heard has not given me very much confidence that conditions will be much better under this setup. I sat in the court and listened to a man who was making his plea. He had hired a lawyer to present his case. The chairman said to the man, "How much is your debt?" The man replied, "It is $800 and I have paid back
Farmers' Creditors Act

$650." "How much do you owe now?" asked the chairman. The man said, "I owe $1,100". "What do you want done about it?" The man replied, "I would like to get it down to six or seven hundred dollars." The chairman said, "What would be the good of that? Can you pay it off then?" The man said, "I think so. I work hard and want to get it cleared off." "When are you going to pay it off?" And the man replied "Just as soon as I get a good crop and a good price." The chairman said "When are you going to get a good crop?" "I do not know," the man replied, "it will be as soon as the Lord sends rain." Then the chairman asked, "When are you going to get a good price?" But the Minister of Finance was not there to tell him that.
It is not the farmer's fault. He labours on his farm. Why should all the risk be taken by the farmer? Why should labour always take the risk in that way? Does the farmer deserve no protection for all he has done in those years when he did all he could? I hold no brief for the farmer who is dishonest or for the man who will not work. Those things can be proved, and if a man has been found to be deliberately dishonest or unwilling to work I would say, let the courts take action in such cases. But where it has been proved that a man is not guilty of these things, he has a right to be secure on his land and to some recognition of the fact that he has toiled on his farm for practically a lifetime. Why is it that the law will permit a man who has paid all but a few hundred dollars of his debt to be foreclosed, and the creditor to take everything, recognizing nothing of those years of labour and toil which that man has put in? The same applies to a good many city dwellers, men who having bought a home, perhaps mortgaged the place to get the money to buy it, and have paid off all but a few hundred dollars when the property is foreclosed and they receive nothing. These things are wrong.
Let me also point to some of the adjustments which have been made under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. The minister may not know what kind of contracts the board sometimes makes with farmers. Here is a typical case: first, to get the farmer where he owes a couple of thousand dollars which he cannot pay under existing conditions; they then reduce it to $1,500, which also he cannot pay under existing conditions because he is not getting parity for his produce. They say, "Well, you sign a sort of crop-lease agreement. Under this one-third of your crop for the next three years is to be delivered to the creditor; we will sell it and the value will be credited to you, part to pay interest, and if anything remains, the

balance to pay part of the principal. Then at the end of three years a readjustment of principal will be made on that basis. After that, for the next three years you are to pay three per cent of the principal and all of the interest. For the next three years you are to pay five per cent of the principal each year and all the interest. For the next three years you are to pay seven per cent of the principal and all the interest, whether you get a crop or not"-except in certain bad years where adjustments may be made-"and the next year you are to pay the balance of the principal and all the interest that is due, which is 55 per cent of the principal and all the interest." What does that amount to? Ais well as that, there are certain regulations which state that the creditor shall tell the farmer what he shall grow; how he shall farm the land; how much summer-fallow he shall put in each year. It may be that in the thirteenth year, when the farmer has to pay 55 per cent of the principal, the creditor will tell him to put in all summer-fallow so that he shall have nothing with which to pay the 55 per cent. That is a common settlement under the act, and that is why farmers do not flock to get all their debts adjusted under this set-up. It is nothing less than a thirteen-year sentence of servitude with a boss ordering you around and in the end you are to be foreclosed.
I suggest that, if you want to make this act something which will work, all farm debts, where application is made, should be adjusted after there has been a search to determine the extent to which the present debt is a result of crop failure, and in years when the farmer has no production over and above enough to sustain his family, no interest should be charged and there should be no interest charges compounded. Also, all excess charges which have been loaded on this farm debt should be carefully checked. When some of these mortgage and loan companies get a farmer in debt and send him a bill of what he owes on his mortgage, it makes interesting reading. I have here a copy of a bill which was sent to me, and which includes these items: first of all, interest, $320; interest on interest; insurance premium; another years' interest; interest on interest; interest on disbursement; interest on account January 1; inspection fees. Then he had to pay these amounts every year: interest on interest; inspection, $5; hail premiums, $29; insurance premiums, $28; interest on "loan sundries" to date-whatever those are-$320; interest on interest $37. All the inspections and other items which are set down here grow larger and larger. Interest climbs up, plus inspection

Farmers' Creditors Act
fees, solicitor's fees, long distance calls and so forth. No wonder farmers' debts grow. When not paid, these are compounded.
In all contracts there should be a clause which permits a farmer who makes his living on that land to have some basic living costs which he can hold back, something on which his family can live decently. If you recognize that claim, it will be at least a step forward. There should be no interest in those years when his production does not bring him a sufficient income for this.
Further, I would say that there should be a provision, effective while the war is on, prohibiting foreclosure on any farmer whose son or hired man has been taken away from him, as has happened in so many cases. Foreclosure should not be permitted in respect of any farm where the state in this time of struggle has had to call upon the farmer to send his boy to the armed forces, or any such man who goes voluntarily. Surely those men who are willing to go and fight should receive legislative protection at least to the extent that there should be no foreclosure or issuance of writs permitted against their farms during that time or when the farmer is not allowed to deliver the produce of his toil. I have had cases of this kind in my own district. A farmer came to me and said, "Look at this. The sheriff is threatening to issue a writ against me, and I have to deliver that grain; yet the government tells me I cannot deliver it." As a result of a little correspondence I finally got them to say that they were not going to proceed with the business of foreclosure,' because the farmer had the grain on the farm and could not deliver it, but he would have to pay the cost of issuing the writ.
I say to the minister, make some alterations in this bill in the interest of those who work and produce the good things of the world. Do something which will save these people in time of stress. Put a little real justice in this bill. If this government does not see its way to do that, it is time that it made way for a government that will.

I wish to speak briefly on the principles of this bill and to support those principles, because I believe that they are advantageous to the farmer. I acted for farmers for twenty years before I went into politics. I expect to be acting for them many years after I am out of politics. I am only a small-town lawyer; I have no interest in the big interests or financial barons or the Dominion Mortgage and Investment association;- I am interested only in the farmers of my constituency.
I was surprised at some of the attention paid this afternoon and this morning to memoranda
and statements and briefs submitted by the Dominion Mortgage and Investment association. I certainly do not think these briefs merited anything like the attention which my hon. friends have given them.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: We were judging by the results in the bill.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am judging by the results of the bill. This is a bill not framed in the interests of financiers but framed entirely in the interests of the farmer.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) interrupts. He based his stand, as I understood it, on three points. One was that the courts have been substituted for the boards of review, and that in this way the costs would be increased and the sympathetic attitude which the boards of review had displayed would be lost; second, that there was failure to consider debts as a recurring problem; and third, that there was right of appeal, which would also, according to my hon. friend, add to the farmer's costs.
I am not going to bother to deal with the second of these points, but I wish to deal with the first and third. The second point raised by the hon. member was, as he admitted, a problem really beyond the scope of this bill; it was a problem concerning the whole question of western agriculture, of a market for western produce and of credit facilities. That is a problem, and I am entirely in sympathy with him so far as that is concerned. But it is certainly not a problem that can be dealt with in the consideration of this bill, and for that very reason I feel that ninety-nine per cent of what the hon. member who preceded me had to say was quite irrelevant to the discussion of the bill.
I wish to1 deal with the first point raised by the hon. member for Acadia, as to the courts having been substituted for the boards of review. The first thing a farmer does now under this bill is to file his proposal with the clerk of the court. I do not think for a moment that any member for Alberta would object to that, bearing in mind that these clerks of court have been the local representatives of the debt adjustment board. They are the men appointed by the province who have been acting for years past in the adjustment of debts in Alberta. They are men who know the local conditions and who have had considerable success in working out adjustments. Surely there is no man to whom my hon. friends from Alberta would rather have the proposal made than the clerk of the court. Certainly that is a feature of the new bill which in my view is very much superior to the old act.
Farmers' Creditors Act

From the clerk of the court, who replaces the official receiver, the proposal then goes to the district court judge. My hon. friends from Alberta apparently feel strongly that it should not go to the district court judge. Apparently they would prefer boards of review. I have had considerable experience with the workings of this act during the last nine years and I know how it works in my own area. We have a board of review that comes into the district possibly once a year-it has been usually once every two years. That board includes a supreme court judge, a lawyer, and a member representing the farmers. They come to my judicial district and stay there for about two days. They handle a dozen or more cases a day, often nineteen or twenty. They are not acquainted with local conditions; yet they make their proposals, and then they are gone. I do not think that is as satisfactory an arrangement as to have the proposal dealt with by the district court judge who is resident in the district, who is acquainted with the district and acquainted largely with the farmers of the district, and who has a responsibility and a duty to that community.
I would point out this to my hon. friends. When they are dealing with a district court judge they know exactly what they are dealing with. They are dealing with British justice, which has been hammered down over the centuries. When you are dealing with British justice and a Canadian court you know what you can expect. You know you can expect justice and fair play. I emphasize that, because there is a fundamental difference between a judgment of a court and a decision of an administrative board. Remember that a board is not bound by rules of evidence; it is not bound by court procedure. All that a board has to do, as I recall the law, is this: it must not act in a manner offensive to the general principles of justice.
I would point out that even the boards of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act had the right to hold and did hold meetings in secret, which is not permitted in any court of law. They heard confidential evidence, received confidential reports on the value of the land, and had the authority to receive and did receive confidential reports on the character of the farmer; and acting for that farmer you had no right to see that confidential report as to the value of the land or the confidential report as to the character of the farmer. That offended a fundamental principle of law, the main principle which all courts follow, that no man shall be tried or have his case determined without the right of seeing and hearing the evidence upon which

he is tried or upon which his case is determined. There is a fundamental difference between a court and a board, and I find it strange and hard to believe that any hon. member, or anyone purporting to speak for farmers, would say that he would prefer such treatment for his farmers to the open and above-board treatment which the farmers can and do receive and must receive in any court of law.
The hon. member for Acadia said that the cost would be increased by this procedure of taking away the board1 of review and substituting the court, overlooking entirely the provision in the bill which states that no costs shall be payable.

That is their privilege; it is there. The hon. member for Acadia referred to an argument which had been advanced, I believe he said by a mortgage association, that the act should be limited to efficient farmers. He should pay no attention to a contention like that, but he submitted it to the house. The hon. member went on to say that only dishonesty and rank idleness should be barred under this act. I think the act goes even a little farther. I do not think anything short of that is barred when it states that a proposal shall be based upon the present and prospective capabilities of a farmer to meet his debt, consideration being given to the productive value of the farm. That is the principle which is laid down for the guidance of the district court judge.
The district court is an inferior court, and in rendering his judgment the district court judge must show jurisdiction upon the face of his order; he must show on the face of the proposal which he makes that it was based on these considerations. The act certainly goes far enough to take care of most of the inefficient farmers. It takes care of the inefficient farmer on a good farm; it takes care of the efficient farmer on a poor farm; it considers the capabilities of the man and the productive value of his farm. It is not the productive value of that farm as joined to some other farming unit, or some other circumstances; it is the productive value of that farm as worked by that farmer, with his limited capabilities.
I do not think there can be anything stronger or fairer than that. I would expect that those opposed to this act would say that the provision goes very far. I think there can be brought under the provisions of the act the farmer who is idle, the farmer who may be somewhat inefficient, just so long as he has not acted in bad faith in the management of his farm or the disbursement of his income. There would have to be fairly strong evidence to keep any farmer outside those provisions.
My hon. friends object to the provision for appeal. I want an appeal for the sake of the farmer. I am not interested in any mortgage company, but I do want an appeal for the farmer. If that provision to which I have referred was not loaded in favour of the farmer, I might agree that we should not have an appeal. But we have a provision which is loaded in favour of the farmer in that the district court judge must base the proposal upon the present and prospective capabilities of the farmer and the productive value of the farm. The district court judge must furnish the appeal court with a statement of all the information upon which he bases his decision. If a proposal shows on its face that the district court judge did not base his decision upon those ingredients, then I want the right of appeal. I want the right to go to the appeal court and be able to say that the district court judge erred, that he based his proposal upon something which is not favourable to my client. I do not think there is any doubt about what would happen; the proposal would be corrected until it was based upon the foundation set out in the act.
Then there is the question of cost. My hon. friend interrupted me a moment ago to say that there would be certain circumstances under which costs might be given against the farmer.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on the bill in general. I am not going to take very long at this time, because we shall be able to take up the various items in detail as we go along, but generally speaking I think this bill is not as good as the old act, for several reasons which have been pointed out already and into which I am not going in detail. The only feature that I think is perhaps an improvement over the old act is the fact that Manitoba is included. The hon. member for Peace River was speaking of the concessions that were made under a bill passed by the Alberta legislature, and he said he was not concerned about the other provinces but was primarily interested in the province of Alberta. In considering a measure of this kind, I do not think it is proper for any federal member to consider

Farmers' Creditors Act
only how it will affect his own province. Legislation of this kind should be general, and should apply to all parts of Canada. Therefore I think the minister is to be congratulated upon this one point, in any event.
One objection I should like to make is to the fact that only one proposal can be made.
I am not going to begin to recite all the cases I could mention, for I believe I could keep the committee here for a. week if I brought down my files and went through the cases of this kind that have come to my attention. Many of these personal incidents have been pointed out; I think they are very much the same in all three prairie provinces, at all events, so that I do not see that any good purpose would be served in bringing down further cases of the same kind. Supposing a proposal is made which becomes unsatisfactory to the debtor as a result of circumstances over which he has no control. For instance, there might be an emergency year, when the government would recognize that the individual farmer was not to blame for his inability to meet his debts. That possibility is completely ignored under this bill. Surely it is unjust to say there may be only one proposal, and not take into account the possibility of circumstances arising, such as drouth, hail, or destruction of the crop in some other way. Under this act only one agreement or composition can be made. It may be that the farmer undertakes to pay $500 a year in reduction of the principal and interest at five per cent; then it may happen that the farmer is hailed out. How in common sense could the farmer pay that $500 a year? On the face of it that is ridiculous, and I am sure hon. members of this committee will not permit such a provision to remain in the bill. I believe that since this has been drawn to the minister's attention, he will see the absurdity of having such a clause in the bill, and an adjustment will be made. There are many other cases in which the farmer may be placed in a position where it is utterly impossible for him to pay. For instance, in war time he may be a grain farmer, raising wheat, a delivery quota which is set by the dominion government. How can he dispose of sufficient crop to take care of that payment? "Oh, well," someone may say, "when the court is setting this proposal they will consider his quota." But the point is that the government here may see fit to change that quota. For instance, the farmer may have fourteen bushels this summer; then later in the fall the regulation may be changed to the point 'where he would have only a five-bushel quota. Yet the act says definitely that there shall be only one proposal, only one settlement, and that the farmer is obliged to comply with that.
It will ibe seen that the farmer is placed in an impossible position, and that he has no alternative. The proposal has been completed and agreed to, and therefore he has no recourse whatever. I might even go so far as to say that I think this is purely mortgage companies' legislation-and in that statement I want to be fair. As I see it, everything is set to favour the creditor.
Let us review the situation for a moment. One proposal is to be made. I believe it will be generally recognized that when the courts are setting these proposals they will take into consideration the financial circumstances of the farmer, the prices prevailing and the general market conditions. The settlement will be made on that basis. If it is agreeable to the company, they will let it go; and in those circumstances it would probably be agreeable to the farmer. But if it is not agreeable to the company, then the company will appeal. I think hon. members of the committee will understand, generally speaking, that if one has an insurance policy on his car, and has an accident, the general policy of the insurance company is to appeal, or to take the insured to court, if the owner is not satisfied with their offer of settlement. Of course they run the chance of not coming out on top, but they can afford to do that. They may lose some cases, but from the point of view of principle, they will go to the courts. They do that, because in all cases they have one or two solicitors hired continuously to handle their litigation. I am not complaining about that, because it is a matter of good business procedure. But the fact remains that in every instance the company will be in a position to appeal. On the other hand, the farmer is not in that position. It will cost him money every time an appeal is lodged, and he just cannot afford that extra expense.
I believe the principle behind the measure is wrong. Rather than forcing the farmer to pay, the purpose should be to keep the farmer on the farm. Especially in wartime the government, I suggest, should follow the principle of keeping the farmers where they can produce the goods required. One might say, "Oh, well, these will be only occasional cases." But that is not so, when one considers the number of farms in western Canada on which there are mortgages.
The hon. member for Peace River referred to costs. I shall not deal with that point other
Farmers' Creditors Act

than to say that the matter of costs is dealt with in section 37. It is true the section does say:
No costs shall be awarded on any application, motion or hearing before the court or the appeal court-
That is, no costs shall be made on any application before the court of appeal, except -and then it goes on to give some exceptions. So that there may be costs attached to this.

speechtext:
It states:
. . . except that the appeal court may, if of opinion that there were no reasonable grounds for bringing an appeal. . . .
And so on. Of course that is decided entirely by the court. If they contend that there were no reasonable grounds for appeal, the charges will be allowed. So that there is -the liability of paying costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would the hon. member like that exception taken out?

speechtext: No; I think the exception is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I think so, too.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
But the point I am trying to make is that there is a matter of costs to consider. When we start adding costs to a farmer we are placing him in an awkward and difficult position. I shall go on to read the whole of the section, so that it may all appear on the record. It is as follows:
. ; . except that the appeal court may, if of opinion that there were no reasonable grounds for bringing an appeal, order the appellant to pay the costs of any other party appearing on the appeal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: To pay the farmers' costs, if the creditor brought a frivolous appeal.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: And it could be reversed the other way.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It is purely discretionary.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, but the payment of costs depends entirely upon what the court decides in that regard. But to say there are no costs is definitely wrong. However, I shall not discuss further items in the bill, because they will be discussed when we come to them.
One other point I wish to make in passing is the lack of regard given to the western debt conference proposals by those who drew up this legislation. That is very serious, because as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Acadia, that was not a political conference,
(Mr. C. E. Johnston.]
in any sense of the word. In fact, it was about as conglomerate as one could find. There were Social Crediters from Alberta and Liberals from Saskatchewan; and the representation from Manitoba consisted of two groups. Those three governments got together, and after extended and deliberate consideration of the debt problem, from the point of view of the three agricultural provinces, and after a great deal of careful consideration, deliberation and thought, the draft bill was drawn up. I have them before me, but I shall not go into them, because the hon. member for Acadia placed them on the record.
The conference wen-t to a tremendous amount of work and, with one exception, namely where they expressed their desire that Manitoba be brought in, not one of the proposals was accepted. When legislation is especially designed for the three prairie provinces, and when at a conference are found representatives of a Social Credit government, a Liberal government, and another government of combined Conservative and Liberal members; when we find representatives of those groups getting together -and drawing up what they consider to be the type of legislation most suitable and applicable to the prairie provinces, and when we find the government at Ottawa ignoring all these facts, then it seems to me that that is the wrong way to give satisfaction to the people for whom the legislation was intended.

speechtext: I must say to the hon. member for Wellington South that this is the last bill for consideration in committee and third reading; the other bills are for second reading.

May I say this, that these bills have gone through quickly to-night. I* should like to associate myself with those who have made at least some token opposition with respect to the passage of some of them. I am pleased that the hon. member for Wellington South, and some other hon. members who have spoken, have shown at least that this is an independent institution, operating under our parliamentary system. If

Private Bills-Divorce
nothing else has been accomplished to-night in the great rush of legislation, at least through this medium we have established our position, so far as the independence of the House of Commons is concerned.
It is all very well to rush these bills through, but the public does not understand the situation when so many pieces of legislation are going through so quickly. They have no idea that these matters have been dealt with in other places. But, whether they have been or not, I say that does not relieve us or discharge us from our duty of dealing with these bills in this house as we see fit.
In most instances there is no need for opposition to the bills. The terms in respect of them are well understood. Nevertheless I say it is important that this House of Commons shall not take for granted decisions which have been made in other places, or made even by committees of this house. The point now taken by the hon. member for Wellington South ought to be taken into consideration by this committee, if there is any doubt with respect to it. If that does exist, then it ought to be given proper consideration.

I was waiting until these bills had been read before rising to make a similar protest. Some of us have protested about this procedure year after year. This practice is really a reflection upon our whole system of government. To-night I believe we have passed something like seventy-five bills in about half an hour. True, these bills have been discussed in another place, but if we pass the bills to-night we are taking the responsibility for dissolving about ninety marriages. I say that responsibility is one which should not be imposed upon the House of Commons or upon this parliament. It is about time we got down to a consideration of ways and means of removing this blot from parliament itself. I am not one who does not believe that there are occasions when the compulsory living together of people may be a crime against society. But I do say that this method of dealing with divorce cases in Canada is a scandal, so far as this country is concerned, and one which ought to be stopped. I want to join in the'protest made by the leader of the opposition.
I am not so sure that I can support the objection by the hon. member for Wellington South, because I know nothing about the matter. Someone will say, "Why do you not read the evidence?" Well, I must confess I never have had the time to read the printed evidence in these cases. I doubt very much whether any hon. member has read the printed evidence in respect of the cases we have before
us to-night; and I rather suspect that if we did read the evidence in the ninety cases, we would find that in all it was pretty much along the same lines-which, also, I think, is rather a scandalous condition.
I join in the protest which has been made. A similar protest is made year after year. As I said last year, if this were peace time instead of war time, I would demand that every one of these bills be discussed, clause by clause, and passed separately. In that way we might take up so much of the time of the house that the house might eventually decide that there could be another way of handling this problem. To-night we have made our protest again, one which I think is quite proper. As I have said, this procedure is a blot on the institution of parliament, and it imposes upon members of parliament a responsibility which only judges in our civil courts, in the provinces which deal with these cases, ought to have placed upon them. In my opinion this house, in any event, should not be called upon to assume that responsibility.

May I just add one further word. There is no reason that comes to my mind why we should be faced with so many bills at one particular sitting of the house. That is a point which I thought perhaps the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar might mention, but one which apparently he overlooked. We have no right to be asked in an hour's time devoted to the passage of private bills, in the last week of a session, to deal with so many bills. It is impossible to give them the attention to which they are entitled. Without directing any special criticism to the government in this respect, I say that I hope it will not permit this to happen at another session, because it is not fair to the committee and it is not fair to the public, when they read a report of a sitting of this kind.

I am sure hon. members do not wish to have all these divorce bills trailed through the house, and have all this vulgarity and slander discussed before the house day after day. I believe hon. members are looking for some job which we should not have to do. These matters could be left with the senate, very easily, and with our own parliamentary committee. I would seriously object to having this trailed through the House of Commons, and taken up, day after day, before the general public. It is something which should be discussed in camera.

Either we should deal with it, or we should not deal with it; that is my point.

I sympathize with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in the point he has raised. However, I do not know that this is the proper stage at which to raise it, namely when we are discussing the passage of these bills.
I do it every year.

Undoubtedly it would be much better if some other procedure could be found for dealing with these cases, rather than have them dealt with as we deal with them in the house to-day. We could, of course, discuss each bill. There might be some merit in the hon. member's suggestion that we should so tax the patience of the house that some other way would be brought about for dealing with them. But, after all, it appears to me this is not the proper time to raise that point.
In regard to the point raised by the leader of the opposition, these private bills have stood over from time to time. Ordinarily we take an hour each week for the discussion of private bills. But the amount of work which has been brought before the house as a result of the war, including the war appropriation measure, the discussion of which has so far required over twelve weeks, has precluded the possibility of having these bills considered in the ordinary way. That is why they are being considered to-night. I do not think my hon. friend's objection is on very solid ground in that respect.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has mentioned having these cases decided in the courts. I would point out, however, when the courts are mentioned, that any who have visited the courts when these cases have been heard will realize how little consideration is given in those courts. I have seen them go through the courts in two minutes, which is far less time than when they are considered by a committee of this house.

I believe the hon. member for Wellington South was referring to bill No. 88. I would join in his request that that bill be not dealt with to-night, because there are some matters in connection with it requiring further consideration.

In answer to the hon.
member for New Westminster I would say that the last person in public life in Canada who dared say something about the courts, and their consideration of cases, received at once from the Minister of Justice the threat that he would apply censorship. I just tell my hon. friend that he had better watch out.
On behalf of this group I wish to add my protest.
Nine o'clock.

Nine o'clock.
