speechtext:
The house resumed in committee on bill No. 132, to facilitate compromises and arrangements between insolvent farmers and their creditors. - Mr. Ilsley. - Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I had been expressing my regret that the government had taken no notice of the recommendations of the western debt conference in drafting this bill. It seems

unfortunate now that the three prairie provinces went to all the trouble of studying economic conditions in regard to agriculture and calling a convention in Saskatchewan to confer on matters relating to debt adjustment only to find, after all their trouble, that their recommendations received no recognition except in .the one instance by the inclusion of the province of Manitoba.
I had also made reference to the fact that under this bill only one proposal is allowed. Once a proposal is made and the terms of the agreement are fixed, no matter what new conditions may arise, whether it be a crop failure on account of drought, grasshoppers, hail or for any other reason, there can be no revision of that proposal. That one proposal stands and cannot be changed.
The Minister of Finance the other day, speaking of agricultural prices, said that he believed it was next to impossible to set parity prices for farm products, because costs of production varied so much from farm to farm and from province to province. Following the minister's own argument in that regard, surely he must see the discrimination that will result from a bill such as this which provides no opportunity to>
revise a proposal from time to time as conditions change. If, as has been indicated, this bill is to put things on a business basis; if the farmers will have to conduct their agricultural operations on a businesslike basis, surely we must make it possible for the farmers to meet their obligations on a business basis. It is ridiculous to ask agriculture to be the only industry in Canada that is not working on a business basis, not because the farmers themselves are to blame, but because the government refuses to give them parity prices. We must put the blame where the blame belongs. There is no other industry in Canada that is not receiving its cost of production and a fair commission. Take, for instance, the aircraft industry, or the automobile industry, which is now producing transport vehicles for the armed forces, or take a gun factory, or anything you like, and you will find that every one of these industries is working on a business basis and receiving cost of production plus a fair commission. That does not mean that an aircraft plant in Montreal that may be making the Bolingbroke is getting the same price as a Toronto factory making the Bolingbroke, because the costs will vary with each plant. Nevertheless both plants get the cost of production plus a fair commission. Now apply that to agriculture whose costs, according to the Minister of Finance, vary from plage to place and from one province to another. The

Farmers' Creditors Act
cost of production in Saskatchewan may be different from the cost of production in Alberta or in Manitoba, and the cost of production at one point in a province may be different from the cost of production at another point. Yet, if it is possible to give the cost of production and a fair commission to other industries whose costs vary from place to place and province to province, why should it not be possible to do that for agriculture?
Now we are saying to the farmers by this bill: We are going to make a proposal and we are going to make you live up to it. Then I think in all fairness to all parties concerned we must make it possible for these proposals to be revised from time to time.
There is another thing that I think is exceedingly unfair. By section 7 of the bill the cut-off date is made December 31, 1938. Section 7 states:
Where a farmer ... is unable to meet his debts as they become due, if two-thirds of the total amount thereof are owing by him in respect of debts incurred before the first day of May, 1935, he may make a proposal under this act for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement.
If you make the cut-off date December 31, 1938, it is unfair to recognize only two-thirds of the debts incurred before the first day of May, 1935. It would not be quite so bad if the government said that December 31, 1938, was to be the cut-off date for all debts incurred up to that time. I cannot understand why. when the cut-off date is made December 31, 193S, a farmer's whole debt up 'to that date is not included. The proposal here is exceedingly unfair, because agriculture has not had the same treatment as other industries in this country. Since 1938 the farmer has had to pay higher prices for the things he has to buy. He has sold his products at less than cost of production. Surely we should have brought the debt adjustment up to date and made it at least to 1942. I cannot see why we should have brought it up to the beginning of the war and then stopped there. I think the minister should consider changing this section to bring these debts up to 1942; or, failing that, the least he could do would be to make the full adjustment of the debt up to December 31, 1938.
I am not going to discuss the general principle of the bill any longer, but will content myself with dealing with the sections as they come up.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I assume that this is the only opportunity one will have to ask certain general questions that would not arise in connection with the several sections. I
should like to know why the Central Mortgage Bank Act, which was assented to on June 3, 1939, under which the government was given the power to cooperate with lending institutions in the reduction of debt and in providing a considerable sum of money in order to permit farmers to borrow money or to have their debts amortized at a low rate of interest, has not been brought into effect. Under that act the farmer would have been given an opportunity to have his debt written down by agreement; he would have been given the privilege of borrowing money at a low rate of interest; and in that way the measure, operated in connection with the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, would have been of great advantage to the farmers of western Canada as a whole. That act has been on the statute books now for over four years. It represented, I think, a serious endeavour on the part of the government to meet the situation prevailing in the western provinces and generally throughout Canada, and I should like an explanation from the minister why it has not been made operative. Had it been, it would1 have proved of inestimable value to farmers finding themselves in a position where they are unable to meet their debts in full. It would have given them an opportunity to consolidate their debt at a rate of interest which would have made payment possible.

In my opening statement
to-day I dealt briefly with the matter of the central mortgage bank. The language I used was, I think, this:
Due to the outbreak of war in September, 1939, this act has never been brought into force, and it was not considered advisable to implement it during the war years because of the uncertainties which the war interjected into such fundamental matters as the values of farm lands and the real value of farm income. Moreover it was considered that the national credit must be utilized to the full in the prosecution of the war.
When the war broke out it was not possible to foresee what might happen to farm values. A great deal of work was done in valuing farms in western Canada in 1939, and it was on the basis of those values that the mortgages were to be adjusted under the central mortgage bank legislation. Moreover, the act entailed a large obligation on the government. I was not Minister of Finance at that time, and I do not know too much about the central mortgage bank legislation, but my recollection is that it meant a payment of $200,000,000 or something like that to lending institutions.
Then, of course, the act was very controversial. A great many hon. members were

opposed to it; and it did not seem to be the appropriate thing during a war, when values were certainly not static, and when values which farm lands might take on would not necessarily bear much relation to the values set in 1939 for the purposes of the act, to go ahead with the act.

speechtext:
On rising to speak to this particular piece of legislation, I have been wondering whether the farmers of Saskatchewan need to be more on guard against the hon. gentlemen who sit in the two parties to the extreme left of yourself, Mr. Chairman, or the so-called big interests who are pictured as such a plague to western Canada. I feel that those in this house who take the individual extreme case and upon that case paint a picture of utter destitution and utter futility of attempting to cure by reasonable methods the ills of the people of western Canada must alienate to a considerable extent the intelligent opinion of members of this house and of the people generally who reside in provinces other than the three western provinces. I am proud to say that I have followed the course of this legislation with a great deal of interest and with one desire only, namely, to be of practical use and to further the attempt to meet the real necessity that faces the people particularly of my own province.
We have heard about the necessity of this type of legislation. I think the farmers of western Canada themselves would readily

Farmers' Creditors Act
agree that it is a most regrettable fact that this special type of legislation was needed, or is needed or will be needed in the future. But I believe that any fair-minded person who studies the history of the economy of the west, particularly during that period of drouth accompanied by world-wide depression, must long since have come to the conclusion that some particular type of legislation was needed to deal with an extraordinary situation, national in its dimensions and affecting a great number of very fine citizens, and that not only in the interests of those farmers themselves, but in the interests of Canada as a whole some such legislation as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was necessary. And it was, as hon. members know, a Conservative government under Mr. Bennett who initiated this particular act.
I believe, too, that all hon. members can readily understand that at the commencement of a drouth or of a depression period it slowly comes home to all of us that the drouth period or the depression period is going to extend over any great length of time. It is a truism of human nature that hope springs eternal, We all think that this year or next, conditions will again be normal and that the necessity for some special provision will not apply. That explanation is one of the reasons for the type of proposal made by the boards of review which were set up under the act as first passed.
The hon. member for Weyburn, in the first part of his address this afternoon, suggested that it was a judicial sense of appreciation of property rights, but later I believe he gave the real reason, namely, that it was simply a combination of inexperience and failure to appreciate the job that had to be done that gave rise to the incompleteness of the early proposals. Simultaneously with the introduction of this act in fact before this particular act was passed, as one would expect, the legislatures of the three western provinces, being closer to the problem, introduced their debt adjustment legislation, which operated unquestioned for a number of years. Even to-day, despite the fact that the privy council has ruled that the Alberta act is ultra vires and, as a result, the legislation of the other two provinces is likely to be in the same position; notwithstanding that decision, I say, in my province the creditor class goes to the debt adjustment board for the necessary permission to initiate any proceedings. It is clear, therefore, the act that was passed in my province worked to the reasonable satisfaction of both the creditor and the debtor class.
There was, however, this profound differ-ance between the two types of legislation.

The provinces never claimed any right, except possibly the province of Alberta, but certainly Saskatchewan never did claim any right to cut down compulsorily either the principal or the rate of interest in any contract. It realized that it did not have that particular power and authority. This act passed by the dominion authority did give the tribunals entrusted with the administration the power to reduce both principal debt and interest. We all know, despite the willingness of the creditor class generally to cooperate with the provincial legislation, that it would be highly inadvisable to rely on legislation upon which the privy council had passed an adverse opinion. Some day somebody will claim in the courts the right to question the validity of the act and, as a result, will be granted a favourable decision. So that I naturally, with other western Liberal members, followed with close interest the attempt of this authority, the dominion, to deal reasonably with the problem that was thrust upon it as a result of the privy council decision.
In the first place, it has already been called to the attention of the committee that this government has passed an order in council which provides that under an agreement for sale or under a mortgage the court with jurisdiction may stay action if it sees fit, or may postpone the payment of the debt, or, if the occasion arises, may vary or extend the order, all for the purpose of retaining the farmer upon the land. That order in council was very important to us, and we are assured that it is the intention of the government to permit that order in council to remain in force for the duration of the war.
We must, therefore, consider what the' dominion government has done, under the provisions both of this bill and of the order in council which has been in force throughout the three western provinces. A number of members, particularly from Alberta and also from my own province, have referred to the submission made by the three western provinces after the conference on debt and have suggested that the government has made no or very little attempt to carry out the recommendations of that conference. Let us examine just what the three provinces recommended in principle. They recommended "that a tribunal or tribunals-be created by the appropriate legislative-authority in Canada, first, to write down the-pincipal of farm debts, secured and unsecured"; that is to be found in this bill; second, "to reduce the interest rate on farm debts, secured' and unsecured"; that principle is to be found in this bill; third, "to alter the terms of payment of farm debts, secured and unsecured";: that principle is to be found in this bill.
Farmers' Creditors Act

Fourth; "to review and revise its own decisions in the light of events subsequent to the making of the decision." Western members have pointed out frequently that one of the things that caused irritation in the administration of the act was the fact I have referred to earlier, that decisions were made by those who were inexperienced or, as the hon. member for Weyburn has said, timid in approaching the problem of actually making a proposal. It was Considered extremely unfair that those who had come before were subject to the terms of early proposals that were not properly fitted to take care of the debtor's position. It is true that *this bill does not go so far as to give to the new tribunal the power to review every proposal made by any board of review, but I think it goes a long way. It gives to the new tribunal the power to review any proposal made 'prior to December 31, 1938.
All of us know that 1937 was probably the most disastrous year that came to western Canada. Since that time our farmers have not been offered credit on anything like the same scale, and very few have been able to get into any substantial amount of debt since that particular period. In addition, a great many farmers have learned the lesson that getting into debt is a much easier task than getting out. I think, having in mind all the circumstances, the provisions of the bill with regard to review substantially grant the requests of the three provincial governments. In any event it is a distinct improvement over the old act and, if circumstances and time prove that it is not sufficient, then parliament still remains one of our institutions to which we can come and present our case again.
Fifth, "to extend to individuals in any particular year or circumstances the protection of any of the provisions of this legislation available to any debtors, whose affairs are being administered under it." This bill does not meet that particular request, and it seems to me that this legislation could not possibly deal with that. We would' have to' be prepared to bring in special legislation to deal with solvent persons who happened to meet a particular difficulty that might require assistance of this kind. Sixth, "to stay proceedings arising on debts or securities after an adjudication has been made"; that provision is in the bill.
Seventh, "to make the foregoing remedies available with respect to any farm debts regardless of the time at which they were incurred." Again the bill only partly grants the seventh proposal. As hon. members know,

that particular request would make this legislation a continuing act, applicable at any time to farmers who had got into financial difficulties. The bill provides that any debt, two-thirds of which were incurred before May 1, 1935, may be brought before the tribunal. The bill goes farther in that it gives consideration to the fact that one of the contributing factors after 1935 to the difficulties of the farmers was the accrual of interest. Possibly two items, interest and taxes, would go a long way to make iip a very substantial portion of all new debt incurred by western farmers after May 1, 1935. The bill provides that included in the computation of this two-thirds of the debt shall be not only the mortgage principal but the interest that has accrued upon the mortgage or the agreement for sale, whether it occurred before May 1, 1935, or afterwards. In connection with taxes we have provincial legislation dealing with this particular matter. It is not nearly as important as that of accrued interest on mortgages and agreements for sale. Again I submit that the government is to be commended upon going a long way to satisfy the request made in the seventh clause by the provincial governments.
I may say that when making presentations to the Minister of Finance with other western Liberal members we tried to persuade the government that the time had now come to recognize the peculiar conditions under which farming was carried on in western Canada, and while at the moment'-we had not then the news of the drouth that is now appearing in western Canada-farming conditions were reasonably good, common sense told us that sooner or later we would again have a drouth period in which the farmers might face difficulty. I have had always in mind the primary need of getting this legislation through parliament-I use that word advisedly, having in mind that parliament is more than the House of Commons-and I know that a great many people, in eastern Canada particularly, would not be in favour at this time of passing permanent-type bankruptcy legislation aimed directly to satisfy farmers' needs. When we consider the real advantages that are being offered to farmers of western Canada by the amendments contained in this bill I believe we can feel a sense of healthy appreciation of the difficulties which have been presented and a realization that the problem has been approached in a realistic way with a desire to go as far as possible along the road toward the solution of these difficulties.
I accept in toto the arguments of the hon. member for Peace River with respect to the

Farmers' Creditors Act
change in procedure. I do not look upon that as a loss to the farming community in which I live but rather as a distinct gain. I have in mind that, as he pointed out in connection with Alberta, the clerks of the court have been the provincial representatives of the debt adjustment bureau in Regina for a great many years, during which time they have gained considerable experience in negotiating settlements between debtors and creditors. They are now made the official receivers under this measure. Their experience; the fact that they are completely detached, in all personal respects, from both debtor and creditor, should enable them to be of considerable help in bringing about settlements before matters reach the district court judge or the appeal court. I believe also, with the hon. member for Peace River, that the fact of the district court judge being available to hear all such applications, and to deal with them as quickly as possible, will be of benefit as well. If, perchance, there should be any interlocutory applications necessary under the provisions of the act, he is available to hear such applications, which should be of great advantage to farmers who unfortunately have to take advantage of the protection of the provisions of this measure.
Then, as my hon. friend pointed out, and in this I wish to support the argument of the hon. member for Lake Centre, if the appeal judge is chosen wisely; if he undertakes the permanent task of going through a certain territory-my own province, for example-ironing out differences which may arise in the interpretation of these provisions by the various district court judges, making the application of the act uniform, giving every farmer who comes before him the full protection of our courts, with all the precedents that bind those courts in matters of fairness and justice, the farmers whom I represent will get a great deal more service under this particular measure than they could ever hope to get under the old act.

speechtext:
I do not think that is the explanation at all. This measure has had two advantages. In the first place it has dealt with the applicant for relief, and in the second place it has acted1 as an inducement to the creditor class to make voluntary settlements with their debtors. As my hon. friend knows, I come from the very heart of the drouth area of Saskatchewan, and I can say to him that in the last year or two there have been many settlements of debts as between debtor farmers and the creditor class. I am very happy to say that. I agree, however, that when the mortgage companies say that fact alone is sufficient to justify the repealing of all such legislation, they miss the whole point, which is that a year or two of reasonable prosperity in regard to both production and price levels cannot possibly hope to take care of the debts which have accumulated over a great many years. I always regret when the finanr cial houses of this country place themselves in opposition to measures which would meet some of the real problems with which our agriculturists are faced. I am quite certain these companies do themselves no service by attempting to influence parliament from dealing fairly and reasonably with the farmer class. As a creditor myself I am absolutely convinced that it is a good thing for the creditor class as well as the debtor class for us to get this terrible structure of debt brought down to a position where the farmer may regain his hope of paying it off, by harnessing himself to that job. In the long run it will be found that the creditor class will benefit, together with the farmer class, when that position is reached, and that is what we are attempting to accomplish.
Someone in the Social Credit party, I think, said it was impossible for any farmer in western Canada to pay off his debts. Let me give the hon. member one example that came to my notice when I was home at
Farmers' Creditors Act

Easter. I recall a farmer coming to my office about four years ago, telling me his troubles and asking if I thought he should go under this act. I knew the man well; he was an old-timer and a first-class farmer. I said, "No, I do not think your financial position warrants your going under that act." Then he asked if I thought he should quit-claim title to a particular half-section of land. I said, "No. We are in the depths of the depression as far as agriculture is concerned. It can only improve; it cannot get worse. Stick to it; you are a good farmer, and if things break a little better, you will come out on top." When I was home at Easter that farmer was able to report to me that he had1 completely wiped off the debt on that particular half-section of land. This does not mean, however, that man is living in wealth and luxury. As someone has pointed out, farmers throughout Canada for many years have had to practise thrift to :a degree which I do not think is consistent [DOT]with the fine profession they follow. Nevertheless there are men in western Canada who are making progress. The situation in regard to the payment of current debts proves that; and the large reduction in past indebtedness is also an evidence of that fact. Unless we meet another period like that which we went through from 1930 to 1939, we shall find that the debt structure will be steadily reduced. Nevertheless, that problem is there; and I say to the mortgage companies and to the creditor class generally that they would be doing themselves a service if they would join with those of us who take a reasonable attitude in this matter, who do not aim for the moon but who strive for an act that will be reasonable in its provisions to both creditor and debtor, in order that conditions in western Canada may become much improved.
Finally, .while I have unsuccessfully urged upon the government the adoption at this time of a measure designed to meet permanently the conditions under which the people of my province have to carry on farming, I am aware that more and more our legislation must recognize that out west we do not work on the basis of an annual turnover but rather on a much longer cycle; that periods of drouth are followed by periods of very good production, and our economy must take that into account. I hope that some day this or some other government will recognize the need and give us legislation of the kind I have mentioned. I would say to the minister also that I endorse everything that was said by the hon. member for Peace River in regard to section 33, for I think this section detracts from what I have said with regard to this bill. I do

not think the section is wise or practicable, and I think the act would be greatly improved if this section were removed. If, however, for reasons which I cannot appreciate, the minister does not feel that this section can be wholly removed, I sincerely hope he will give consideration to amending it to make it not applicable to proposals that have been made hitherto, and that the period of five years may be reduced to two years.

speechtext:
There are certain general observations I should like to make, while this particular section is before the committee. Ordinarily one would hesitate to occupy the time of the committee, particularly at this late stage of the session; but when one stops to consider that a matter of such extreme importance as this has been introduced during the dying days of a session, then I for one feel thoroughly justified in taking whatever time I consider necessary to discuss the matter.
Those of us who come from the west represent, in the main, agricultural sections of Canada. We come in daily contact, weekly contact, yearly contact with the farmers, and we have been able to develop an understanding and an appreciation of the difficulties confronting them, not for a period of only one year but throughout the years. Personally, I would feel extremely remiss in my duty if I were to permit this opportunity to pass without expressing my views.
Before doing so, however, may I say I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Swift Current indicate that the government of Saskatchewan knew that authority to pass a debt adjustment act did not rest with that province; because I have in mind the important part the government of Saskatchewan played when the Alberta government appealed against the disallowance of the Alberta acts. If I am not mistaken, the attorney-general of Saskatchewan proceeded to England in that connection. I was also disappointed that the hon. member did not discuss more fully the recommendations of the western debt conference with respect to the recurring aspects of the farm debt problem.
If my understanding is correct, I believe the recommendation was that these debts would be reviewed every five years. When one stops to consider our general economic instability as applied to agriculture, and when one recognizes that from time to time most unexpected things occur, he will realize that it is not the proper thing to place a farmer in a position where he is obliged to accept a proposal for settlement, and then, regardless of conditions which may develop in the

Farmers' Creditors Act
future, he must still abide by the terms of that settlement. I think, when we consider this aspect of the measure, all we have to do is to reflect upon those cases which were considered shortly after the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act became effective, where we found farm debts reduced by approximately sixteen per cent, and where, later on, owing to experience, I have no doubt, on the part of boards of review, and also on account of conditions which had developed, the average reductions amounted to approximately thirty-four per cent.
From time to time we have protested most vigorously about the fact that those farmers who came under the act, in the early years of its operation, were not permitted later on to have a further adjustment made. I cannot agree with the point of view opposed to the recognition of the recurring aspect of this debt problem. I would have been pleased if the hon. member for Swift Current had given us some indication of how we should treat debt created during the drouth period around 1936 and 1937, since the provisions of this measure will not give any consideration to that aspect of the problem.
I consider the farm debt problem one of the most important with which we have to deal, apart from the actual prosecution of the war; although it is an integral part of our actual war effort. The future of our basic industry will depend very largely, if not almost entirely, upon the nature of the legislation we pass at this time. Every industry in Canada, every business in Canada and, I dare say, every individual depend directly upon agriculture for existence. Therefore, in the light of that statement, it is not difficult to appraise the importance of agriculture in our national economy. The history of the farm debt problem is not fiction. I believe there is not an hon. member in the committee who is not thoroughly familiar with the difficulties encountered by our western farmers, especially in the past decade. We characterized that period as our pre-war depression, when the majority of western farmers worked without pay. I say that they worked without pay because the prices which prevailed during those years hardly, and in many instances actually did not pay the cost of production. I know that during all those years practically nothing was done to correct the condition which had developed.
It is a well known fact that many of our farmers exhausted their credit and had to assume the position of serfs. That is not an exaggerated assertion. All we have to do is reflect upon the conditions which developed in our own communities, and give a moment's
consideration to the many farmers who either had to leave their farms or accept the position of tenants or serfs, operating those farms for someone else. I know that even in 1931, before we entered the most difficult part of the depression, only fifty-two per cent of our Canadian farms were free from debt. Therefore we could say that only fifty-two per cent of farms in Canada were actually owned by the individuals residing upon them. I know some may argue that if a small debt rests against a farm, that does not change the indi-. vidual's status with respect to ownership. However, I cannot agree with that.
I know also that in 1931 about one out of ten of our Canadian farmers were tenants- and I use that term because some may take exception to the word "serfs". I do not know exactly what the picture was between the years 1931 and 1942, but we do have sufficient information to come to the conclusion that fifty-two per cent of our farmers resided upon farms in 1931 upon which there was no debt. That percentage had been materially reduced by 1940. The reason for that is obvious.
I say it is evident that there are certain organizations in this country which evidently welcome a trend toward this condition which I have described. It would seem that there are some who feel that if the individual occupies the position of tenant, being less independent, he may be more easily manageable. I have a quotation which I should like to give from a bulletin issued by the United States department of agriculture, entitled "Getting established on the Land", and I quote it because I think it is quite applicable to our own country:
Thousands of farmers, large and small, have been unable to keep their heads above water under the impact of adverse forces since the world war. The small owners, burdened with debts, faced with competition, selling their products at low prices when depression hit, toppled into the ranks of the tenants. Tenants on the other hand found themselves squeezed out time and again as landlords were forced to cut them loose to find work as day labourers, if possible.
Very frequently we discover that becoming a tenant on the land which a farmer formerly owned is just one step toward having to leave the farm completely. I have always asserted that the finest situation which could develop for agriculture in this country would be to have the farmer own his parcel of land under a set of conditions which would guarantee that, as long as he was willing to play his part and do his best, he would continue to be the owner of that property.

Would the hon. member concede the same for every other man in Canada?

If I say that a fanner should be guaranteed a set of conditions which will enable him, as long as he plays his part, to remain the owner of his property, I would say that it is perfectly true so far as the business man or storekeeper and others are concerned, provided, however, that the individual does not engage in practices which are detrimental to his fellow men. I have in mind probably a monopoly which develops and exerts its evil influence upon the lives of a great many of our people.
We know many of the debts of our Canadian farmers were incurred while money was plentiful and while prices of the produce they raised were relatively high. I know it is often argued that if you make money available to farmers or anyone else, they will take it whether they need it or not. But that is a weak argument. My contention is that when many of our farmers secured loans, the prices of their farm produce were high and they had every expectation, in the majority of cases I know, of being able to repay the debts even at the rates of interest they had agreed to pay, which often were exorbitant. I believe that the large majority of our people are honest, but frequently we judge them by the very few who indulge in questionable practices. Many of those persons who secured loans while money was plentiful, were obliged to try to pay it back when money was scarce. All we have to do is to contrast prices in 1929 and 1933. The farmer who borrowed money in 1929, when wheat was standing at a fair figure of $1.40, was confronted with a most deplorable situation when in 1933 the price of the same wheat had dropped to about 34 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern at Fort William, and we know many farmers received as low as ten and twelve cents for the quality of grain which they grew. We must recognize and appreciate a position of that kind.
But the farmer struggled- on. He was exploited in many respects. I should not like hon. members to take any wrong inference from my use of the word " exploited." I have in mind, for example, that farm machine prices went up and up and up, while produce prices went down. The farmer was also confronted with an increased tax burden in many instances, and I would even include in my term "exploited" what I regard as price manipulation. The farmer during that period lived in constant fear of losing his home. I had the opportunity of spending about one-third of my life in a community where the farmers were probably having more than the usual difficulties. I do not believe there was anything with which they were confronted that created

more desperation in their hearts than the fear that to-morrow or the day after they might be evicted from their property. We have heard that one of our goals after the war is to be freedom from fear, and I would be hopeful that it would apply not merely to a crosssection of our population. No industry except agriculture, manned by the hardy fighters of the-calibre of which our Canadian farmers are, could have survived the treatment they received during those years, and I definitely state that it is a credit to those people for putting up the fight which we all know they did put up during that period. The agriculture industry survives, and therefore we hear certain people advancing the argument that, if it survived once, it will survive again, and probably again and again. But while agriculture survives, there is not an hon. member here but would agree that it was badly crippled. However, in spite of the fact that it was crippled, it performed magnificent achievements when it was called upon to do so following the outbreak of war in 1939. Not only has it continued through the following years to make great achievements; it has also been committed to the tremendous task of providing foodstuffs for the countries of Europe which have been subjugated by the enemy. In spite of all that, regardless of the farmers' magnificent achievements, the best that we seem able to do is, first, pat them on the back, appeal to their patriotism, and tell them what fine fellows they are. No doubt the Minister of Agriculture has devoted a good deal of energy to patting our Canadian farmers on the back and appealing to their sense of patriotism-
Mr. LaFLECHE: Getting them markets.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
-in order to have them continue to carry on this magnificent production. I am not forgetting, with regard to the interjection, the unsatisfied markets here, during the depression years, When the farmer begged to sell his produce and the people begged for it, -but we seemed unable to solve the problem. But I say we must give our Canadian farmers immediate assistance through adequate debt adjustment legislation. If this government will not do it, who is expected to? We know the provinces have tried, and we know the situation which they are confronted with. I am not endeavouring to argue as to whether the' province has the right or not; I am simply asserting that if the province has not the right, the federal government has not only the right but the duty to do it.
With respect to our western debt conference, it is significant that, as has already been indicated by previous speakers, three of our

Farmers' Creditors Act
prairie governments, supported by quite a number of organizations, submitted a comprehensive debt adjustment proposal, and I regret that the government has not seen fit to give greater consideration to it than we have done. I am not one who is going to condemn the present bill. Surely, if you cannot have all you want, it is better to take something rather than discard it all. But I am hopeful that while this bill is in the committee stage, the government will be prepared to accept certain amendments.
We hear the argument frequently advanced that farmers are now paying their debts. The hon. member for Vegreville indicated to-day that when the farmers-I speak of the great majority of them-can pay their debts they will do so. I recall one branch of the Canadian Legion indicating to me, "We are not asking for charity; all we are asking for is an opportunity to pay our debts." It is right that the farmers are under present conditions paying their debts. But is it not unfortunate that we should go along through these desperate years and then have to have a war to partly solve our problems for us? This war, we hope, is not going to last long. If it comes to an end this year, let us say, I wonder what situation may develop? When someone speaks of the farmer paying his debts during war time it brings to my mind a little report which I saw in the Ottawa Journal. It reproduces a report which appeared in the Carbon Chronicle. Carbon is a little town in Alberta. The item, reprinted from the Edmonton Journal, states:
J. A. Hannafordi, of Howie, Alberta, sold a carload of steers last week for which he received $3,000. Six years ago he sold a similar carload which netted him $300.
The Edmonton Journal comments:
No w-onder a lot of Alberta farmers are reported paying off farm debts now, and' little wonder they were unable to do much along that line some six years ago.
I read that for two reasons: it indicates that our prices have definitely improved and that farmers are paying their debts; it further gives a very fine reason why many of them plunged hopelessly into debt during those so-called depression years.
I do not wish to take a great deal more time, but I say that our debt adjustment legislation must be evolved, not in the light of these abnormal conditions which we are passing through now, but in the light of previous experience and also of the situation which we may reasonably expect to develop from time to time after the war. I am quite in agreement with those who have urged that there is only one sensible manner of preventing colossal debt within the framework of the agricultural industry, and that is for us to endeavour to lay down a national agricultural policy. Only through a national agricultural policy can we establish that industry on a sound and prosperous basis, and only by laying down a sound policy can we hope to see agriculture occupy the position which we shall expect it to occupy during the post-war reconstruction period.
I do not think it at all unreasonable that our farmers ask for parity of price. Surely there cannot be any argument against a farmer's demand that the price he receives for his produce should bear some fair relationship to the commodities which he is obliged to buy and the taxes which he is compelled to pay. I say, furthermore, that unless we can establish some scheme whereby our farmers can secure credits in order to carry on their operations at lower rates of interest than many of them have been obliged to pay, we shall have a repetition of the conditions which developed.
In addition to proper debt adjustment legislation, which must come, we must have adequate marketing facilities. I am not thinking so much of the present moment as of the period to come when I make that assertion. The hon. member for Swift Current indicated this evening that you cannot quote one case and try to arrive at some principle based upon that case. I have the particulars of one case which I believe is significant. I say it is significant because this farmer, who is a good farmer, agreed to pay, not so much cash every year, but one-half of his total crop. He lived up to his obligations 100 per cent, and what, Mr. Chairman, do you think his situation was? On October 12, 1926, this man bought a farm made up of 324 acres at a total cost of $13,766, which was approximately $42.50 per acre. He made a cash payment of $2,000, and the remainder was to be paid, as I have already indicated, over the years by giving one-half of his crop and paying interest at the rate of six per cent. *This man did not miss one payment. By 1935 he owed over $13,000. Do not forget that he had paid $2,000 to start with and was giving half of his crop; yet in 1935 he had approximately the same debt he had started out with. Prices in 1926 when he started were: wheat, $1.51; oats, 49-6; barley, 63-9. These were the average. But before 1935 had arrived wheat was 54-3; oats 26-4, and barley, 32-2. That was at Fort William, less approximately seventeen cents a bushel, and he did not grow No. 1 grain. He was forced to sell feed wheat at 104 cents and feed oats at 7 cents. In 1935 he went to the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. They were "very kind"

Farmers' Creditors Act

and reduced his debt to $12,000. Do not overlook the fact that he had paid $2,000 cash and half his crop every year from 1926 to 1935, and yet they reduced his debt to $12,000.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I do not take up much time in speaking in the house, but I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion of bill No. 132, and while I agree with much that has been said, I disagree with some. I disagree with any implications that have been thrown out to the effect that western Canada is down and out. Western Canada is not down and out, and I think I can give a few facts that perhaps will be illuminating to some hon. members.
Hon. members from Saskatchewan have every right to speak of conditions in their province and so have those from Alberta to speak of theirs; but I claim the privilege of saying a few words with regard to debt conditions and reductions as regards Manitoba, that good old province of which I have been a resident for over thirty-two years, and which I think I know at least as well as any other member of the house.
I wish to speak first of reductions in debt that have been made by the Manitoba government, and I shall go to the best source available, to the remarks made in his budget speech

Farmers' Creditors Act
last April by the premier of Manitoba, who has also been treasurer of that province for a good many years. These are some of the facts he disclosed, speaking of the public debt. He said that on April 30, 1941, the gross public debt of the province was $126,000,000, and that during the year ended April 30, 1942, the province had paid off $2,500,000 of that debt. Then he said that on April 30, 1942, the gross public debt of the province had been reduced to $124,000,000. He went on to say that the further reduction from May 1, 1942, to December 31, 1942, amounting to $1,267,000, reduced the gross debt to $123,000,000. He added that in the thirty-two months ending December 31, 1942, the gross debt of the province had been reduced by $7,000,000. Those are the words uttered by the former provincial treasurer of Manitoba, now the premier, in his budget speech.
I should like to add a word as to the municipalities. I have not the figures for last year, which were undoubtedly more favourable than those for 1941 which I shall quote. There are 170 municipalities exclusive of cities, with an annual levy of about $8,000,000, on an assessment of $238 million, being a rate of 34 mills. During 1941 no less than 151 of these municipalities operated on a cash basis; that is, they raised the money and they paid cash. There were only nineteen out of the 170 which had deficits at the close of the year. What about their debt reduction? Records show that between 1935 and 1941 they reduced their debt by $7,000,000. Municipal reduction was $7,000,000; provincial government reduction, $7,000,000. I think that is an extremely good showing for any province, a showing of which the people of that province might well be proud. At the end of 1941 there were 108 municipalities out of the 170 which had cash surpluses of over $1,000,000; and, in addition to that, they had special reserves in cash or investments, other than sinking funds, of $661,000. The mortgage foreclosures for Manitoba were as follows:
1928	 395
1933	 397
1941		 128
1942		 106
I think those figures constitute a record of which Manitoba might well be proud. But what about discharges of mortgages? Here, again, I think the figures will be illuminating. Premier Giarson is authority for the statement that in 1942 there were 5,432 farm mortgages discharged, paid off, wiped out. In other words, in 1942 there were 106 foreclosures as compared with 5,432 discharges, a ratio of fifty to one. Why was this possible? As the people drew
72537-322J '
away from the awful years of the drouth and heart-break, they set themselves resolutely to the task of applying their increased income to reducing their indebtedness. What about farm income? They were in a better position to reduce their indebtedness, and they did it. Here are the round figures for farm income:
1938		 $ 62,000,000
1939		 63,000,000
1940		 64,000,000
1941		 80,000,000
1942		 100,000.000
We must not forget that the outlay of these farmers was considerably increased because they had been compelled to let their equipment run down during the drouth years; their buildings had got into disrepair, and many expenditures were needed. If these had not been necessary, they would have been able to reduce their mortgage indebtedness still farther.
Something might be said with regard to improved methods of farming. Manitoba, more than any other western province, has adopted diversified farming and, strange as it may seem, the farm income last year from wheat was only one-quarter of the total income. Then, again, I would not have hon. members forget that some of this mortgage indebtedness reduction is owing to the fact that the dominion government paid to the farmers of the west in the form of bonuses and payments of one " kind and another some quite substantial amounts. From August 1,1941, to July 31, 1942, $14,000,000 was paid in prairie farm assistance; $34,800,000 in wheat acreage reduction, and $18,000,000 in prairie farm income. There was a total in one year of $67,700,000, without including expenditures on prairie farm rehabilitation.
I wish to make my position clear in a very few words. I bow to no man in my support of the farmer or anyone else who finds himself down because of reasons over which he had no control. I am not one to stand idly by and see a man or his family almost down and out and treated with unfairness, sometimes with downright cruelty. We do not want that, and our citizens are not going to stand for that sort of thing. On the other hand, I am not one who will stand up and see the creditor defrauded by the double-crossing of some dishonest or oftentimes defiant debtor. We want to see fair play and justice in this country, and I am satisfied that the members of this committee will agree one and all with what I say.
I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that consideration should be given to the creditor who, by reason
Farmers' Creditors Act

of age or infirmity, has taken up residence in town and is operating hi3 farm perhaps by crop lease or hired help. That man should receive some consideration for himself and his life partner. Many of them have had some crushing experiences under the old act, and we do not want to see those repeated under this act. We should protect these unfortunates who, owing to crop failures or other causes over which they have no control, are likely to suffer. We do not want to sweep away the whole fabric of confidence in this country. Manitoba, and the west in general, have developed by credit, and that credit has been based upon confidence. Any hon. member or any individual who would sweep away that confidence is doing his best to bring a tragedy upon this Canada of ours. I believe the average man is fundamentally honest. I believe the average man is a square-shooter. I ibelieve the average man wants to hold the *confidence of his associates and will agree -with the sentiments I have expressed. But in speaking of confidence let us not forget that western Canada has been built up on a feeling of confidence, and in past years perhaps there was too much credit, though I may be mistaken. In a certain committee of which I have the privilege of being a member we have heard many references to post-war problems, to the new order for which we all long, to the treatment our boys should receive when they return from overseas, and so on. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that all these things will require money, and a lot of it. If we are to raise that money, we must retain the confidence of the people, young and old, rich and poor. I do not think I could find better support for this view than in quoting again from the conclusion of that budget speech delivered by the premier of Manitoba, who said:
We have not reached the limit of our development in this province. A great deal still remains to be done. If there were no other reason, much still remains to be done in order that we may reach full emplo3rment in the post-war period1. If we are to have rural electrification or housing or a direct connection through Manitoba with the Alaska highway to attract tourists or if we are to have a multitude of other things for which public expenditures will be required, there are only two methods by which the province can make the money available; in some cases by taxation and in other cases by borrowing in order to spread the cost over a period of years. No matter how heavily the people may ask to be taxed for these worthwhile purposes, some of the moneys required will still have to be raised by borrowing. Whether we can get this money will depend upon our credit. This is true no matter what

the means of raising it may be. Whether we can get it from the investor in the open market will depend upon- his faith in whether or not we can be trusted to repay him. If some less orthodox method of making the money available is provided by the Dominion of Canada creating credit at no interest cost, as recommended by some citizens in our country, then we still would have to be considered reliable before even on such a basis the dominion government or any other body such as the Bank of Canada, would lend us money at no interest or low interest.
Finally and most important of all, the Manitoba government must have credit with Manitoba citizens. Our own people of Manitoba must consider that their provincial government will carry out its promises and undertakings. If we are going to have any worthwhile post-war projects we cannot hope to succeed if we do not have the active cooperation of Manitoba citizens. Rural electrification, for example, will not be a success if the farmers of this province, relying upon the government's ability to carry out its plans, do not make preparations to receive and use the power which is delivered to them. We may wish to ask them to buy some of our bonds for this purpose. I suggest that if we had broken our promises and ruined our credit, we could not expect the Manitoba people to buy our new bonds in the face of our having defaulted on our old ones. Moreover, we could not then expect them to take our post-war plans at face value, because they would have a right to doubt and would doubt whether we could find anybody who would trust us with the means of financing such plans. Doubting, they would not make their own plans to cooperate with their provincial government in a project in the completion of which they had no genuine faith.

I wish to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance upon the calibre of the bill he has sponsored, which I think will receive wide endorsation from one end of Canada to the other.
